speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head S of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, our workforce is ageing and growth is slowing to zero gradually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we must have as high a workforce participation rate as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our female workforce participation rate has improved over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When women have at least one child, the participation rate drops by 10% to 16% compared to women with no children in 2018.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This suggests that caregiving responsibilities reduces workforce participation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Labour market factors, such as men being over-represented in higher paying occupations such as managing directors, chief executive officers (CEOs) and general managers accounted for roughly 7% of the gap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The natural question is why not more women are taking on such top jobs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some academics attribute this to women not taking on higher paying roles that tend to demand for work to be prioritised over personal responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Women are also increasingly better educated than men in Singapore, especially in the younger age brackets; 64% of females aged 25 to 34 years old have university education compared to 56% for men.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There has clearly been progress over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What the adjusted gender pay gap means too is after adjusting for education, age, occupation and industry, women in Singapore earn on average 6% less than their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This difference is magnified when we consider disparity over a 40- to 50-year-long career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to a Ministry of Manpower (MOM) study in January 2020, the authors stated that even though the model can explain for more than half of the unadjusted gender pay gap, the unexplained component could reflect the effects of parenthood, caregiving responsibilities and unmeasured employment characteristics, such as work experience, firm type and job scope as well as discrimination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The same study also observed that more women are primary caregivers, and this could be one of the reasons for the gender pay gap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In essence, the increase in caregiving responsibilities could have resulted in women exiting the workforce and also getting paid less.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to tackle this structural problem of the gender pay gap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I agree that it is multifaceted as the 2020 study has noted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Conceptually, the human resource practice of performance grading could have inherent biases against women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, if there is a good performance grade to be given and the choice was between two employees, both are as good but one was away on maternity leave for 16 weeks, which employee would be more likely to get the good grade?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The organisation should rightly reward the employee who had contributed more over the full year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we can imagine that if this persists over multiple childbirths, and promotion depends on multi-year performance consistency, then we can imagine a mother's progression being derailed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It seems plausible that this could have resulted in women and mothers not being able to scale the heights of their professions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must guard against such well-intended human resource practice driving unintended biases against women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is perhaps what we call the "motherhood penalty" and we owe a duty to doing right by our mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The solutions are not easy to come by.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the Equal Pay Standard, companies must undergo a certification process every three years, during which they are required to analyse their wage structures, identify and rectify any gender-based wage disparities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Failure to comply can result in fines and sanctions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While this might be too bold a move for us at this stage or it needs to be contextualised to our needs, there are other steps that we can take.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, there must be greater disclosure and transparency in the gender composition of senior management roles and compensation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some employers are rightly concerned about wage transparency, but we can do so like today when board directors' fees are declared in broad tiers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can start with the listed companies in the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Greater transparency and reporting requirements can spur organisations to review and improve or change their practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage HR practitioners to examine and improve upon the performance evaluation criteria that have embedded undue biases, for example, ranking a mother on maternity leave with other colleagues on the same basis is inherently biased.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are entrenched societal norms of women in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Women often bear a disproportionate burden of caregiving responsibilities, and this can be at the expense of their careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we help them to manage their careers and caregiving duties?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This caregiving is beyond those required for children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must support our women better, offer affordable childcare, flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and flexible caregiving policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have, indeed, made strides in ensuring affordable childcare and I look forward to the release of the tripartite guidelines on FWAs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that we can also consider implementing leave policies to support employees in caring for elderly parents, particularly considering Singapore's ageing population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employers have reasonable concerns because there would already be too many leave provisions when manpower is already tight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The reality is maternity and childcare leave consumption will continue to decrease because of our low total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The statistics also show that caregiving can take a worker out of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some have questioned if a few days of caregiving leave could make a difference?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My answer is yes, because it underscores our commitment to helping our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have to start somewhere, no matter how small the first step is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we must remember that workers' caregiving responsibilities will only increase in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers need our support to care for their dependents, young and elderly alike.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I wish to call on all businesses in Singapore to take concrete steps in re-examining their leave policies and consider offering caregiving leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Closing the gender pay gap requires us not to only confront the societal and caregiving expectations of women, but also the structural barriers that limit women's economic opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, next, I will speak on supporting our older workers to stay gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have spoken on the importance of harnessing the experience and expertise that our older workers bring to the table, especially in light of our ageing demographics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have made significant strides in raising the retirement and re-employment ages for Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry clarify how many percent of these employees were offered re-employment contracts of one year and whether the re-employment contracts were subsequently extended?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On training our older workers, the findings from NTUC's survey conducted in 2022 underscore the keen interest older workers have in upscaling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Re-employed workers might get even less training opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On another front, as training participation declines with age, it is crucial to implement age-universal job redesign strategies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ironically, older workers actually need more training because their odds of skills obsolescence are higher.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The PW Mark was implemented to distinguish employers that have leaned into providing progressive wages voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can consider distinguishing progressive and inclusive employers which have significantly improved their business processes, training and job roles to help older workers succeed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Incentives can be provided to such employers, especially in the absence of the WorkPro.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, what might our future workforce look like?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, it will become more intergenerational because our population is ageing, and people are working and staying in the workforce longer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, because of more rapid technological changes than ever before, the difference in backgrounds, mindsets and skillsets across different generations will become sharper.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, there will be more churn in our future workforce for all of us, again, because of the pace of change.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our economy must allow for creative destruction to stay relevant and vibrant, but for the individual, churn in one's career is tumultuous.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Third, there will be a greater need for our future workforce to engage in agile and deep learning throughout life to deal with churn.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We must create a pervasive culture of learning and skilling throughout life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fourth, amid these challenges, there will be growing needs for FWAs because our family structure is getting smaller and so, caregiving burdens are more concentrated on individuals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, our knowledge of care itself has become more advanced, whether it is for seniors, special needs or mental health.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the caregiving demands of tomorrow will be far greater and we need FWAs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fifth, our future workforce will be increasingly cross-cultural because there is simply not enough Singaporeans and we will need human capital from around the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Amid this confluence of complex changes, how does MOM plan to develop a future-ready workforce that is more intergenerational and cross-cultural, more prepared for a new normal of churn, more engaged in agile and deep learning throughout life and more flexible in its work arrangements?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Chairman, at last year’s MOM COS, the Manpower Minister announced the setting up of a new feature in the MyCareersFuture portal known as the CareersFinder.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Perhaps because of his medical background, he couched it as a tool to keep tap of our career health, very much like physical health.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When I heard of it last year, I thought it was a refreshing approach to encourage workers to take stock of the state of their career health, starting with better insights and awareness of our own employability situation and thereafter, taking proactive and purposeful steps to keep career health in good shape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This new feature is particularly important and useful to those in their mid-careers who tend to be more career vulnerable and hence, need better career agility and resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In my conversations with those in their mid-careers, many have concerns on the durability of their current skillsets and jobs and how the fast-paced technology advancement, such as AI and blockchain, would impact their jobs and career development.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In that context, can I ask the Minister for an update on the CareersFinder beta?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How has the take up been and has it achieved the outcomes intended?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, as a whole, how can the various career health initiatives benefit individuals, employers and the economy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Nevertheless, can I ask if the Minister can share the broad principles and the parameters that will be featured in this new scheme?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Has the Government taken in feedback from the public and as well as the tripartite partners in the design of the support scheme?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some countries have practised some form of support for the involuntarily unemployed but many end up with poorly designed unemployment benefits, which can inadvertently make it more attractive for involuntarily unemployed workers to stay unemployed rather than to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How has the Ministry incorporated learnings from these countries and feedback from the public and tripartite partners in the design of the upcoming support scheme for involuntarily unemployed jobseekers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the anticipated average duration of support required for the involuntarily unemployed?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that while the support scheme must assist the involuntarily unemployed, it does not make it more attractive for the involuntarily unemployed workers to stay unemployed?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we ensure retraining and upskilling using SkillsFuture credit and actively searching for jobs including compulsory attendance for career, curriculum vitae and interview coaching be prerequisites for support?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the medium term, wage increases can only be supported along with productivity increases.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we need to continue assisting employers in creating an environment conducive to workers' training to increase workers’ productivity and support employers to realise enhanced firm productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are MOM's plans to support our employers to do so?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet there are many challenges faced by employers, such as escalating utility costs and increasing manpower expenses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I wish to highlight the shared responsibility of consumers and employers in supporting lower-wage workers here.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the strategies to enhance consumer awareness of the PWM Mark to bring the consumer's role to the forefront in supporting businesses committed to fair wages?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore must maintain its openness to talent and uphold global connections, particularly amid declining local labour force growth stemming from our ageing population and low birth rates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we remain open, it is crucial to continuously review and calibrate foreign workforce policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we ensure that these policies contribute to Singaporeans' real wage growth?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is it timely to establish clearer distinctions between various work passes based on the specific job appeal to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alongside these distinctions, should we adjust the dependency ratio ceiling to ensure that enterprises have the necessary manpower to thrive while ensuring equitable access and higher wages for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to note that existing foreign worker levies, LQS and the PWM are effective levers to support higher wages for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The persistent challenge of not being able to send workers for training due to manpower shortages necessitates a nuanced approach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach allows time for local workers to engage in training, leading to overall improvements in human capital development within firms and maximising Singaporean workers' growth potential.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Programmes, such as SkillsFuture Level-Up, and various improvements to SkillsFuture, are a key pillar to empowering Singaporeans to take up good jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With enhanced SkillsFuture funding, the challenge is to ensure that employees, while in their jobs, can identify and acquire new skillsets aligned with corporate objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) without an HR business partner (HRBP) role may face difficulties in corporate alignment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Chief HR Officer (CHRO)-as-a-service can be a solution to mimic the HRBP role and maximise the translation value of SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The increased disruption in job scopes highlights the need for improved job redesign capabilities, especially with the support for acquiring new skills in Budget 2024.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Developing measurement tools and benchmarks for equitable assessment of salary ranges for newly acquired skillsets is crucial.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to support employers to drive transformation by redesigning jobs for new and emerging opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Job redesign can also help to assimilate older workers as they reach retirement and extend their working duration.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with FWAs, it will create the nexus for a future-ready labour market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I would like to ask MOM how we are empowering employers to re-design jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How are we empowering workers to improve their career health?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Recent stories about ongoing retrenchment and redundancy exercises in companies, such as Lazada and Electrolux, have only intensified discussions in public about retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Generally, benefits upon retrenchment depend on the company's policy of severance package and retrenchment benefits, as well as the terms of the contract of employment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast to our prevailing practice, many jurisdictions around East Asia have enshrined both the right to some form of retrenchment benefits and the amounts to be paid.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For instance, under Part 5A of the Employment Ordinance in Hong Kong, both the right to severance payments, except in cases of dismissals, and the amount of severance payment to be paid are enshrined in legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Malaysia regulates both the employment termination and layoff benefits regulations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thailand's Labour Protection Act also determines the severance pay amount for workers depending on their employment period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: South Korea grants full-time employees severance pay under the Labour Standards Act regardless of reasons of termination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taiwan sees employers liable to pay severance pay under the Labour Standards Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indonesia has a minimum statutory severance and long service pay.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In general, such payouts are close to a month's wages for every year of service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, I asked the previous Minister of Manpower how it ensures companies pay retrenchment benefits that meet industry norms as defined by the tripartite standards for companies that retrench workers for reasons not related to financial distress.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It called to ensure that they are rewarded fairly, since these workers contribute to our collective higher standard of living.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, we should also look at mandating retrenchment benefits for workmen and employees covered by Part 4 of the Employment Act to start with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some groups I mentioned are the most deserving among us with wages below the median and it is crucial that we pay special attention to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Legislating their right to retrenchment benefits would be one concrete way of supporting workers in the name of Forward Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their median salary is $2,700 and their median age is 56 years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The low wages, ageing workforce and heavy reliance on foreign labour in this crucial sector is concerning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge the efforts by MOM, industry associations, unions and institutes of higher learning (IHLs) to professionalise these trades.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, attracting young Singaporeans remains a pressing challenge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To overcome this, we need to first boost societal respect for the skilled tradesperson, or "tradies", as they are affectionately called in Australia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Schools and trades associations can create greater public awareness about what tradies do.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are not all dirty, difficult and dangerous jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, licensed plumbers often do more supervision and inspections of plumbing works than the dirty work themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Young people who prefer working with their hands should be encouraged to consider skilled trades instead of forcing themselves to study an academic subject they have little interest in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, we need to lower the barriers for entry for Singaporeans to become licensed tradespersons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All courses and mentorship programmes leading to licensing should be more subsidised under SkillsFuture, even for workers under 40.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And more places should be set aside for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, to raise incomes of skilled tradespersons, agencies must rigorously enforce regulations against unlicensed individuals performing tasks that are legally reserved for licensed tradespersons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will uphold the required quality and safety standards and prevent licensed tradesperson's earnings from being unjustly undercut by unlicensed competitors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look towards building a resilient and future-friendly workforce, it is crucial to recognise the invaluable contributions of skilled tradesmen in essential professions like plumbing, electrical work, air conditioning servicing and mechanical repairs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our skilled tradesmen and women have forged fulfilling careers over the years, but as Singapore transforms itself economically over the years, these are taken for granted, but essential trades are at risk of a diminishing Singaporean worker base.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to make these trades exciting to attract new talents, such as youths and mid-careerists.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To achieve this, we must provide clarity on the career pathways for those entering the skilled trades.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that master tradesmen are forged from a blend of strong foundations in theory and practical unique ground experiences, it makes sense to reintroduce the apprenticeship programmes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Apprenticeships can offer clear milestones and support to progress to the next levels.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes opportunities to attain certifications, licences and eventually to become master-level tradesmen.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Clarity on career progressions is essential as many may not be aware of the potential for growth and advancements in this field.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How would the Ministry further the career progression model through tripartism?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would the Ministry further their work with trade associations and guilds to not only highlight the career paths available but also in articulating clear wage and career progression levels?

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad that we have seen a series of enhancements to SkillsFuture at Budget and at MOE's COS debate earlier.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), especially those above 40 years of age, are anxious about the prospects of their employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have three suggestions for MOM to bolster SkillsFuture to empower Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, with the new growth sectors and crafts and to meet the needs, passion and interests of Singaporeans, especially PMEs who are looking at career conversions, can MOM consider expanding the range of courses and programmes beyond the current suite of Career Conversion Programmes (CCP) offerings?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, mindset shift training as well as career coaching and counselling are key to reducing unemployment and under-employment and increase employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope as we strengthen the career health of Singaporeans to provide greater support in this space, including to employers and placement arms and intermediaries, such as e2i.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I wish to ask MOM for the status of the strengthening of the Singaporean Core efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am aware that work for the Workplace Fairness Legislation is under way.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, human capital practitioners, practices and processes are key to foster a fair and inclusive workplace, including one with a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am aware IHRP is doing good work to certify human capital practitioners with the IHRP certification, as they are also the national Job Redesign Centre of Excellence, to help companies, including through their human capital diagnostics tool, to level up companies' practices and processes and productivity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can MOM progressively mandate the certification of HR practitioners with the IHRP certification?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And in the interim, perhaps companies should have at least one IHRP-certified HR professional before they can be allowed to hire foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think the upcoming Workplace Fairness Legislation is an opportune time to push this ahead and perhaps, even incorporate some of these primers on the upcoming piece of Workplace Fairness Legislation into IHRP syllabus, as well as certification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Mr Chairman, with an ageing population and local workforce growth that is slowing to zero, we need to augment our workforce with either more capital or labour, so that Singapore's economy can continue to maintain its vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Without a thriving economy, everyone suffers the adverse consequences of wage stagnation and loss of jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: But we need to do it carefully to maintain the centrality of a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: That must be our unwavering commitment to our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: There have been significant moves, especially the COMPASS scheme and the Shortage Occupation List (SOL).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry update on how COMPASS has helped to support Singapore's economic needs since its implementation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And how has SOL allowed companies to fill hard-to-fill jobs or roles, so that companies can continue to preserve and create jobs for locals?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Our local workforce has also been improving in quality, with median wages increasing annually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The figure increased by 10.5% between 2021 and 2022.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This also means that we need to ensure that our EP holders must not unduly compete against them because EP holders tend to have more work experience and might be prepared to take a lower pay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How would the Ministry adjust the qualifying salary to balance the needs of our Singaporean Core and business needs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What specific SOL jobs continue to lack applications or suitable candidates despite these incentives?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can MOM name these jobs and briefly outline what it thinks could be the root causes of their lacking suitable candidates thus far?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Given that it has been almost six months since COMPASS was introduced, does the Ministry have a view on whether the SOL mechanism is effective as a signal to companies and foreign labour?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: More importantly, for such identified talent shortages, we should also ensure Singaporeans are trained to fill these gaps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In view of the wider-ranging announcements made to the SkillsFuture Framework, including the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, how does the Ministry work with MOE and other agencies, like SkillsFuture, to systematically nudge Singaporeans into these occupations and sectors with training opportunities?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We need to ensure that local workforce development is not just reactive but predictive, aligning closely with future industry needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: These programmes, targeting a mix of US lower-wage workers, high school graduates and young adults, combine training, job placement and support services aiming to transition participants into higher-wage jobs within specific sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Sectors were chosen because of local labour market demand and long-term career prospects, for example, healthcare, IT and manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The success of these programmes was attributed to targeted skills training, certifications recognised within the industry, comprehensive wraparound support services, as well as leveraging community-based organisations with deep local knowledge to facilitate recruitment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In this light, Sir, particularly in view of enhancements to SkillsFuture at this Budget, how does MOM plan to report on the success or otherwise of the initiatives, to improve the employability prospects of the broader Singaporean workforce to fill the strategic gaps in our economy on an ongoing basis?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, there are many industries in Singapore that are growing and competing for local workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: SkillsFuture provides the platform for the current workforce to develop the skills required in the economy and WSG supports with assisting the workforce with job placement and career conversion through programmes, such as CCP.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While we strengthen and provide the opportunity for our Singaporean workforce, we must continue to remain open and connected to support economic growth.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Mark Lee, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, can MOM share insights on which sectors have successfully utilised the Manpower for Strategic Economic Priorities (M-SEP) Scheme and the key lessons and best practices enabling its wider applications?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, is there consideration for allowing firms in the M-SEP scheme to gradually increase their foreign worker quota up to 5%, based on exceeding local hiring or training targets within two years, rather than maintaining a fixed threshold?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the current tight labour market highlights the challenges that businesses across the diverse services industry face.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This sector includes a wide range of businesses, from modern services, like financial, insurance and infocomm service, to lifestyle services, such as hospitality, retail and food services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It also encompasses transport and storage services, and community, social and personal services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The unique workforce composition and varied demand and supply dynamics within each sub-sector demonstrate that the existing one-size-fits-all quota system for foreign workers does not adequately address the specific needs of these industries.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given that certain job roles within the services industry consistently struggle to attract local talent, perhaps a more talented approach to managing foreign worker quotas is necessary.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As such, would implementing a sub-sector specific quota system, addressing jobs like heavy vehicle drivers and certified opticians, be a more effective tool in managing manpower needs, ensuring that areas with persistent low take-up rates by Singaporeans receive the necessary support?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, could the Minister consider initiating a targeted review in selecting sub-sectors of the services' sector, and a nuanced approach can be selected sectors to show overall productivity growth, if given extra manpower?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that workers may still be exposed to indirect discrimination, discrimination-related harassment as well as discrimination by association and perception.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP), which is meant to run alongside WFL, also do not address the types of discrimination mentioned above.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a first step, will it be made clear that all of these different forms of discrimination are prohibited under the guidelines?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Will MOM also commit to a timeline to update WFL to protect Singaporeans from all forms of discrimination at the workplace in the next five years?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On grievance handling, the processes in WFL must be inclusive and accessible to all who may face barriers when seeking redress, whether workers have disabilities or have difficulties navigating a perceived intimidating tribunal system in a language they are not familiar or comfortable with, MOM must pay attention to their particular needs to ensure that they are able to exercise their rights under WFL on an equal basis as others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This also extends to the mandatory mediation and Employment Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More needs to be done to ensure that workers who face barriers are able to access justice if they have been discriminated against at the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Committee further recommended an expansive approach to prohibit all acts done to victimise an individual who has reported their employer for workplace discrimination.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, are workers protected from retaliation for reporting forms of discrimination that are not prohibited under WFL?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can MOM clarify if the WFL's prohibition against retaliation would also protect employees who report their employers to TAFEP for forms of discrimination that are not prohibited under WFL?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This information must be made publicly available in aggregate form.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only with such publicly available basic data on a regular basis could we have a better idea of the problem and move to close the gender wage gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But we can include the prohibition of asking for other information, such as last drawn salary, relationship and NS PES status.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An employer should be exempted from this prohibition only if such information is a genuine and reasonable job requirement, a concept already used in the Committee's final report.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The burden should be on the potential employer to explain why such personal information is needed when requesting the information.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, many countries already recognise the right to reasonable accommodations and the UN CRPD has also called on Singapore to adopt legal provisions to recognise the denial of reasonable accommodation as a form of discrimination, not just in the employment context, but in all areas of life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the issue of retirement adequacy lies close to the hearts of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The recent Forward Singapore initiatives, including the Majulah Package, increased Enhanced Retirement Scheme (ERS) payouts and so forth, are commendable steps towards strengthening retirement adequacy and our social compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They promise support for seniors who need more help, ensuring greater peace of mind, especially in this inflationary environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how these changes and initiatives translate to tangible benefits for citizens, especially for those who require more support?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, the Silver Support Scheme (SSS) continues to play a critical role in ensuring financial support for vulnerable seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, with the rising cost of living, is the current SSS quantum adequate to meet their basic needs and maintain a decent standard of living?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on plans to review and potentially adjust the Scheme's payout to reflect evolving needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These policies represent a renewed commitment to a multi-pronged approach involving the Government, families, employers and the wider community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By working together, we can create a supportive ecosystem that empowers our seniors to retire with dignity and security.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I had previously asked why the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS) did not cover seniors above 70.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I discussed in my speech on the Public Finances Motion early this month, the Government likely earns a higher return from investing CPF savings with GIC than the interest rate it pays to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This difference goes into the Reserves, instead of CPF accounts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hon Member Mr Louis Chua has pointed out in his Budget Debate speech that, over the years, many MPs from all sides have been urging the Government to let CPF members benefit directly from the higher returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can adopt a different approach based on age.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Younger CPF members with more than 20 years to go before their retirement can take more risk for higher returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who are closer to retirement should lean more towards risk-free returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One for risk-free returns as in the current arrangement and another option which incorporates some risk, like pegging to the GIC's annual investment return or other investment options.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Allow younger CPF members who are prepared to take some risk to allocate some of their savings to the latter option, but gradually adjust the proportion allowed downwards with age, so that the portfolio becomes lower-risk as they age.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CPF returns can also be raised through the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS), which was recommended by a CPF panel in 2016 and accepted by the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In November 2023, my colleague Mr Leong Mun Wai asked why LRIS has still not been implemented.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister have since replied on different occasions, that further studies need to be made.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: LRIS can also be implemented in conjunction with my proposal of age-related allocation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The LRIS can be one of the options that takes some risk.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The allocation caps can then limit the risk of this option.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will touch on the closure of the special account for CPF members above age 55.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has said that the closure of the Special Account (SA) is not aimed at saving interest monies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if the SA savings go to the Ordinary Account (OA) instead of the Retirement Account (RA), the Government can be expected to save on interest payments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the amount expected to be saved?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP notes that the maximum amount that CPF members can keep in their RA will be increased four times the BRS.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the reason for capping this amount?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why should we stop CPF members from enhancing their retirement adequacy by putting more into their RA if they wish to do so?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this impose additional cost on the Government?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, I would like to once again take the chance to raise concerns that I had previously voiced out in Parliament over the past three years and also earlier this year, during the debate on our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As described in a poster explaining the benefits of the LRIS, such a scheme involves low fees, is simple and fuss-free.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: CPF savings are pooled together with other members to enjoy economies of scale, investments follow a market index and there are fewer choices and less headache over which funds to choose and does not need active management to adjust risk.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Against the backdrop of inflationary pressures and headwinds in the global investment environment, I hope that the Minister will not respond to this cut calling for the LRIS to be implemented as soon as possible, once again, by saying that he will provide updates when ready, but that he is now ready to provide updates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in its reply to my Parliamentary Question, deposit rates are set competitively in the market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Apart from basic savings accounts, consumers can choose from a range of other savings and fixed deposit products with higher interest rates offered by banks.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Desmond Choo, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Mr Chairman, the recent announcement of the closing of the Special Account (SA) for CPF members above the age of 55 years old has generated much discussion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This is not surprising because of how central CPF savings are in providing for retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: A key factor contributing to its effectiveness is the provision of high and risk-free interest rates on CPF monies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: In a world of financial uncertainty, the CPF scheme offers guaranteed tangible benefits to every Singaporean and bolstering our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This is also testament to the effectiveness of the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Could the Ministry shed more light on why it is timely to make this policy move to close the SA now?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: During my recent house visit, a Tampines resident shared with me that it was logical to earn fixed deposit rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The money should be naturally locked up for longer and not withdrawn easily, as in a savings account.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: However, she was concerned about what her options are, going forward, if she exceeds the enhanced retirement sum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is understandable that residents would want to maximise their retirement monies, especially as we are likely to be in a higher inflation rate but slower growth environment for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry provide more information on its website or other channels on the options that residents could explore if they wanted to get more than the 2.5% from the OA?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The Majulah Package will benefit our lower- to middle-income young seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Together with the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages, it provides for a robust social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is also very good news for caregivers and homemakers, who prioritise the well-being of their loved ones at the expense of putting off their careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: While the Earn and Save Bonus component of the Majulah Package offers support to eligible working caregivers, there remain concerns for those who have not been working or of low income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: First, for the lower income, would the Package allow them to achieve basic retirement adequacy by the time they retire?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Second, for those who are not working, such as homemakers and caregivers, without the Earn and Save component, achieving retirement adequacy would appear to be more difficult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I have two suggestions for the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: First, for the lower-income employed residents: to provide a higher quantum of top-ups so that they can achieve the BRS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The current way of topping up or supporting such residents is via ComCare or other forms of social assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Topping up via work can preserve work ethics and the dignity of work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Second, for homemakers and caregivers: to expand upon the quantum of matched retirement savings, so that employers and family members can help them to reach BRS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This would likely not be enough, especially for those who have been homemakers or caregivers for most of their working lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Such earned or matched top-ups are also aligned with our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Those who have contributed and needed help would be helped by those with more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It also acknowledges the value of unpaid labour and provides them with enhanced financial security in retirement.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) serves as a crucial safety net for Singaporean families, ensuring they can continue to reside in their Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats even if they were to lose income earning capacity due to unforeseen circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: HPS should go beyond the standards set by private mortgage insurers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must expand HPS to ensure that most Singaporeans, including PwD breadwinners with a track record of employment, have access to comprehensive protection of their most precious asset – their home.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOM consider reviewing the HPS risk assessment framework so that more in-need families, who cannot turn to private insurers, get the coverage they need?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: After all, we are talking about public housing, not private properties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They live in their employers' homes and are potentially vulnerable to ill-treatment and abuse behind closed doors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Employers who ill-treat their workers must be punished in accordance with the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, some complaints are unfounded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some employers have been victims of frivolous complaints.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After the worker has successfully entered Singapore at the cost of an employer, the worker makes a complaint in the hope of changing employers or a desire to return home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Based on the accounts of some employers who have been subject to investigations, they did not know what to expect of the protocol or procedures to be adopted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The investigations could take weeks or months, during which, the employer's eligibility to hire a replacement helper would be suspended, disrupting household arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other cases, the decision may be made to take no further action against the employer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, an advisory might be issued to the employer not to commit offences in the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could happen even when the employer was never interviewed by the investigators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does MOM balance the need to safeguard workers' welfare and, at the same time, ensure that investigations are efficient and employers are accorded due process?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will advisories serve as adverse records against employers if they wish to hire other helpers in the future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I suspect that many parents find this insufficient, especially if they have multiple children, each with unique contingencies that could keep them out of school, I wish to speak about how there remains a symmetry between childcare and eldercare leave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As our demographics evolve and ever more children find themselves providing care to elderly parents, they find that there is no equivalent support for them as they ferry their parents to and from medical and related care appointments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially trying for those who are an only child of single children living with their elderly parents, who generally default into the role of being the primary caregiver.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has, unsurprisingly, resulted in caregiving employees facing depression and reduced quality of life, as shown in a 2021 Duke-NUS study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this is disproportionately borne by women, as revealed in a 2019 report published by the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I propose an expansion of family care leave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is an idea that has bipartisan support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Member Mr Louis Ng has tirelessly advocated for paid parent care leave and, if I heard correctly, as has Mr Desmond Choo just now, and so has my former colleague Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it may seem like an additional cost for businesses, the resulting improvement in economic security and well-being of these employees is more than likely to pay for itself in terms of elevated productivity and reduced turnover.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Many in this group of workers will be undergoing perimenopause, which can present various physical and emotional challenges that may impact their well-being and work performance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Awareness of the health-related impact of perimenopause on women's well-being does not seem be widespread in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Straits Times, in a piece titled, "Is Singapore ready for menopause wave from a super ageing society?", interviewed women who quit their jobs or suffered through the pain at work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This loss of productivity may ultimately be costly to businesses and the economy, not to mention the human toll it takes on female workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is notable that the United Kingdom (UK) and Australian Parliaments have convened Member of Parliament-led consultations to raise awareness nationally.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In Singapore, we can start with incentives for women who turn 45 to seek pre-emptive check-ups and for those who need physiotherapy for their joint and muscle pain to either subsidise the treatment or give them time-off for it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: If women are forced to cut short their working life during their menopause transition, their health and finances may worsen and our economy will lose out on their valuable contributions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The implementation of FWAs is critical in this support and we see tailwinds with the adoption of the tripartite standards for FWAs and the upcoming Tripartite Guidelines for FWA requests.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, many caregivers seek employment to cover expenses for dependents, like individuals with disabilities or seniors, often needing jobs with FWAs due to caregiving demands.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In exchange for greater flexibility in schedule, caregivers sometimes settle for low-paying roles that may not match their education levels or skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The financial strain of caregiving can be great, especially if they have had to quit their jobs or reduce their working hours to be a caregiver.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This problem is particularly pronounced where the caregivers are single.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And for caregivers who are single, whether there is additional support for them?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: FWAs have become a key consideration for caregivers and senior workers deciding to stay or return to the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: It is arguably also a rising consideration for younger workers who choose to work flexibly so as to pursue side gigs and taking on higher degrees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As more employers embrace FWAs and as the dust settles on the implementation and proliferation of FWAs, it is important that fair workplace norms be created in the support of win-win employer-employee outcomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Employers must see productivity gains in the introduction of FWAs and employees must be fairly assessed and treated when it comes to performance appraisals, work assignments and their requests for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Beyond acceding to more family care and caregiving leave, which may prove to be untenable in the longer run, employers see FWAs as a more sustainable way to support their workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, it is important that for true sustainability, FWAs be rolled out in planned, managed ways so that productivity is not impacted and trust continues to be built between employers and their workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: To this end, what will the Ministry be doing to further equip and support our companies in the redesign of their job roles and in the re-engineering of their work cultures?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some companies have also expressed their concerns as service providers in third-party outsourcing business sectors, such as cleaning and security.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: They have shared that while they hope to implement FWAs in their industries, which faces manpower crunches, service buyers may continue to stick with more traditional contracts that are not outcomes-based.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: How will the Ministry be promoting and closing this gap as we move towards FWAs as a nation and economy?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Indeed, the need for job redesign is critical in the role of FWAs to fair worker outcomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The Women and Family Unit of the NTUC has been advocating for FWAs, long before COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In the earlier days, some industries have pushed back citing reasons that the nature of their job types make FWAs untenable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This includes jobs in healthcare, services and manufacturing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: They too include part-time work, doing remote work from a regional office and flexible hours.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I am glad to note that post-COVID-19, our Healthcare Services Employees Union have partaken in a pilot to introduce flexible loads and flexible timing for our healthcare frontliners in hospitals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In the wide-scale introduction of FWAs, how will the Ministry encourage more sectors to roll out FWAs creatively and fairly?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, as Singapore's population continues to age and birth rates decline, it has become increasingly important to support the physical and financial independence of our seniors in order to ease the economic burden on the workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The good news is that with better education and skillsets, we would expect to see seniors open to staying economically active for a longer time, whether for financial reasons or just to stay active, with 41% of the labour force now holding at least a university degree, a significant increase from just 27.6% in 2010.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: However, seniors who are not pressed financially may like to work part-time after retirement to balance leisure time and professional engagement for a healthier pace of life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Others would like to reduce work hours due to health reasons and supplement retirement income against rising costs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: What plans are there to support older persons who are willing and able to contribute to work but with reduced hours?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, today, I want to focus on two key aspects of building a more inclusive workforce: harnessing the potential of senior workers and fostering FWAs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: First, as Singapore's population ages, raising retirement and re-employment ages is a positive step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: However, maximising their potential requires more than just extending their tenure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Ministry share plans to support structured career planning, re-employment opportunities and job redesign to harness the potential of senior workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Second, FWA unlocks true inclusivity in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I commend the Public Service for leading the way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: It is encouraging to see more companies implementing diverse and sustainable approaches since the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: These include work arrangement autonomy, flexible hours, compressed workweeks, remote work and job-sharing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The key message is this: output, not location, should matter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: FWA empowers a diverse workforce to thrive, regardless of personal limitations or preferences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: However, extending flexible work opportunities to the frontline, shift and blue-collar workers present unique challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: To truly foster inclusivity, can the Ministry share on strategies that cater to diverse roles and responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This could empower individuals like caregivers, PwDs and others who require flexibility to join or remain in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Looking at Singapore's best employers ranking list, working from home is clearly a key factor, with Google topping the list for its hybrid work arrangements even after the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Let us move beyond simply offering FWA as a benefit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Let us strive to make FWAs the norm, accessible to everyone regardless of their profession or position.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, I am heartened to see that while we work on growing our economy and equipping our workers with the right skillsets, we are also focusing on strengthening our social compact by ensuring growth is inclusive and with work-life balance for workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: FWAs will be a key enabler for this, but it must be done in a way which balances the needs of both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: FWAs can be in the form of flexible time, flexible place and flexible load.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Have our guidelines moved the needle for hiring them?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How do we assist companies to manage FWA requests while maintaining harmony, fairness and productivity in the workplace?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, the NTUC U Women and Family and PAP Seniors Group collaborated recently to conduct a survey for Singapore residents above the age of 50 who are currently working.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Most of those surveyed were in favour of raising retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, these are real concerns among the older workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: PAP Seniors Group has been engaging with many of them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Bukit Batok East, I also received feedback and appeals from more senior workers who feel that they are not given the job just because of their age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At times, they feel gradually cast aside at work and were eventually asked to leave on the pretext of poor work performance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A lot has been done by the Government to change attitudes, including by giving employers incentives to hire senior workers and supporting the redesign of jobs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could the Ministry share some of the latest efforts and plans to continue building a conducive environment for seniors to participate in the workforce?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should leverage on the voices of advocates who care about the plight of older workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also more enlightened employers who have good practices that should be emulated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What more can these employers and community partners like seniors groups do?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can they meaningfully champion the cause and amplify their efforts?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, every senior should be given the opportunity to decide how they wish to live out their older years.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some may choose to retire at a suitable point, others may desire to continue working for a few more years or perhaps find meaningful engagement in serving the community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In order to have the ability to make choices, financial considerations will be one major factor.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some seniors may need to work a little longer to build up enough retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Employers need to appreciate the experience and value of seniors in various vocations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: To all employers currently providing job opportunities for seniors, thank you very much.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I am encouraged to learn that one of the recommendations put forth by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness involves the issuance of a Tripartite Advisory on providing reasonable accommodations to individuals with disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It is imperative that individuals with disabilities are not unfairly excluded from job opportunities simply because they require reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: These accommodations are crucial for both employers and employees to achieve their full potential and drive business success.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: They can encompass a variety of adjustments, such as physical modifications, changes to job tasks, technological aids as well as fostering understanding and support from colleagues.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While some employers may view reasonable accommodations as optional, we must recognise that for PwDs, these accommodations are essential for their livelihood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Insurers obtain premiums paid for by employers and have incentive to keep costs low by limiting insurance payouts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: How long have insurers taken to process claims, for example, and how many claims have been rejected?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, businesses in sectors such as creative, media, coaching and delivery have evolved their business models to tap freelancers as the main labour pool.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These businesses prefer freelancers for their expertise and responsiveness.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They also prefer freelancers for efficient budgeting as labour can then be reflected as a unit cost.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Oftentimes, the commoditisation of freelancer services meant that businesses were conditioned to find ways to spend less on freelancers as a component.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This included holding back from providing injury coverage to freelancers, whether by direct insurance or by preferring freelancers who include the cost of injury insurance into their fees.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The commoditisation of freelancer services also means that at work sites, businesses might prioritise business needs over the health and safety of freelancers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, post-pandemic, it was common to hear of freelance production crew working on shoots for 16 or more hours at a stretch, just so that the production house could compact filming into one day and thus save on venue and equipment rental costs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Upon shoot completion, these freelance crew must still make the trip to return the production equipment, thus many might only call it a day after nearly 20 hours at work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Should a freelancer get injured during work, past cases have shown that it could be very trying to obtain compensation from the business for the freelancer’s medical bills and downtime.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially difficult if the freelancer was injured badly because of the work or work conditions.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While the tripartite standard on procurement of media freelancers’ services urges adopters to provide insurance for freelancers on set for injury and gear damage, this is not a pervasive practice.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise for freelancers who provide exercise coaching or delivery expertise, they are often instructed to adhere to work instructions set out by service buyers and intermediaries.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the course of work, they might injure other persons or property by accident.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Again, it is seldom that the service buyer and intermediaries provide the freelancer liability insurance via direct coverage or by engaging freelancers whose fees have factored in liability coverage.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A lack of injury and liability insurance thus exposes the freelancer to risks that he or she is not equipped to deal with.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This could mean that the service buyer and intermediaries provide the freelance service providers with injury and liability insurance via direct coverage or engages freelance service providers who already possess coverage of such insurances.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As businesses continue to restructure and de-risk, it would take collective will and guardrails than mere goodwill to ensure that workers, whether employees or freelancers, are valued as contributors and their safety and health at work is regarded and prioritised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, I wish to raise the issue of predatory employment contract terms, which many Singaporeans, especially of a younger disposition, may be unknowingly entering into.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: To better protect our Singaporean workers and educate them on their rights to fair employment and rein in errant employers who make use of unfair terms in employment contracts to gain advantage at the cost of employees' well-being, it is critical to examine some practices and review whether we need to re-examine our stance of not introducing regulations against these.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Some examples of these unfair or predatory employment terms are in the position of early termination fees, training recovering fees, replacement fees and other financial penalties that arise when an employee decides to leave a workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: These terms are often justified by employers as necessary to protect their commercial interests, but in practice, restrict the avenues for alternate employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Another example is in the position of non-compete clauses or restrictive covenants into certain employment contracts which do have any basis beyond sharing the same industry segment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, I urge the Government to investigate how prevalent such practices are in Singapore and whether or not they are justified in the ordinary course of business for an employer.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The reality is that even though a contract should ostensibly be entered into by willing parties, the imbalance in economic circumstances and bargaining positions between Singaporean employees and employers leaves little room for employees to challenge such unfair employment terms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Further, employees may not see it as in their interest to embark on their new careers by going through the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) or the Courts before they even start work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As my Sengkang colleague shared in Parliament earlier this year, even if these are unenforceable in the Court of law, the danger is that they have a chilling effect on employee rights even before they can be potentially challenged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Non-compete clauses are included in many modern labour contracts and impose restrictions on a worker joining or otherwise doing business with a rival firm even after employment with the firm in question is over, usually for a specified period of time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Many companies sign non-competes in the name of protecting proprietary knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In addition to the benefits to the employer, employees may also benefit, assured that its trade secrets are safe, the firm may be more willing to invest in their workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Non-competes can also promote efficiency since companies are reassured that knowledge transfer within the firm do not come back to bite them after staff members depart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But non-competes can have detrimental effects on worker rights and freedoms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, the contract literally constrains what an employee can do even after they are no longer employed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Evidence also suggests that it suppresses wages and can depress innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In Singapore, many non-competes have been declared invalid or unenforceable, but restraints have nevertheless been imposed under certain circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, regardless of the law, many non-competes have become ever more common in local labour contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Given the effects of non-competes on the competition in the labour and product markets, policymakers should not abrogate oversight of such clauses to the judicial system alone but exercise an interest in its regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This applies especially to sectors where the frequent movement of employees is a matter of course, such as healthcare and infocomm technology (ICT).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The problem with non-competes is not just about whether or not they are legally enforceable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is instead the chilling fact that the mere presence of such clauses has on employees, especially mid-level ones that may be less familiar with human resource matters and labour protections, when they seek to pursue other job opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What may be worse is absent regulation or guidance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Human resource departments may simply include such boilerplate language in standard contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This inadvertently erodes employee rights and diminishes labour market vitality, regardless of whether they do or do not carry the day in court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The last round of Employment Act review was passed in 2018 and effective April 2019.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: With the rise in median wages, changes in the nature of work, workforce and workplaces, I am asking if MOM will embark on a review of the Employment Act with our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I want to draw attention to three areas which needs to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, there continues to be questions in the interpretation of section 18A of the Employment Act on transfers which impact workers affected by ongoing company restructuring, mergers and acquisitions.
