speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM review section 18A as part of the Employment Act review and issue a set of tripartite guidelines in the interim to provide guidance on what falls within and outside of section 18 of the Employment Act?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, is the provision on "dismissals" under section 14.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: At present, I am aware that employers terminate employees with notice pay but without giving reasons for the termination.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Employment Act currently sets the threshold salary at $2,600 for non-workmen and $4,500 for workmen.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As elaborated by the Deputy Prime Minister in his Budget speech, the wages of lower-income workers have grown faster than the median wage over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is one of the impetus for the increase in the LQS.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It would be useful to give employers sufficient lead time to accommodate any intended changes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, employers of work permit holders have been sounding the alarm bells on surging costs of workers' accommodation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: That is an 11% annual inflation rate, which is not entirely unexpected given the number of migrant workers in the construction, marine and process sectors is 18% above pre-COVID-19 levels and at the highest for all the years MOM has published statistics for.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In the 2010 Construction Productivity Roadmap, the Government set a 20% to 30% improvement in site productivity by 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The final outcome was 19.5% in the decade past.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I understand that there have been no new targets since, with the only productivity related target being the design for manufacturing and assembly adoption in the 2023 Built Environment Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But this is a target for process adoption rather than a target for productivity outcomes per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: A meaningful target is important because it helps us understand how much we can raise productivity before we need to increase capacity for workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Conversely, if, in the meantime, we are unable to increase productivity and reduce manpower reliance as fast as we would like, we need to ensure that companies are able to access adequate accommodation at reasonable standards and prices so as not to have soaring costs passed through to end consumers eventually, which appears to be what is going on now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: MOM shared that migrant workers' numbers cannot keep rising and, hence, the Government should also look to organic ways of retaining talent among work permit holders, which would also improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: One way is to reduce repatriation of workers who have years of experience here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: There are workers who are already socially integrated and have picked up English or even Mandarin during their stay.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Workers who are more familiar with Singapore's work practices can hit the ground running without needing training from scratch.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Qatar has a 90-day grace period after the expiry of a permit during which a worker can change jobs without employers' permission.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We should look to tilt the balance of power to the worker because this is healthy for the industry and workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget Debate speech, I shared about how our policies on migrant workers differentiate between "us" Singaporeans and "them" migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, many workers do not have enough space.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOM ensure that migrant workers have at least the same amount of space as our NSFs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, many workers do not have safe food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) requires all catered food be consumed within four hours after it is prepared and be labelled with a "consume by" timestamp.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers tell me that many of them are catered food without the timestamp and they regularly consume food way past the four-hour time frame.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOM ensure that food catered for workers in dormitories comply with existing food safety requirements?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, and lastly, many workers are made to pay illegal kickbacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Kickbacks are a form of corruption but are punished less severely.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOM increase the penalties for employment kickback offences to be equivalent to corruption offences and have better whistle-blower protections?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Workers sometimes face retaliation by employers when they make a complaint.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Employers can cancel work permits and repatriate the worker.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Currently, employers can decide unilaterally whether to send a domestic worker home or to allow a transfer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Reform of these rules will help Singapore utilise available labour quickly in a tight labour market as well as retain workers who are already here and have the language and work skills to fit in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: After all, workers who have fallen out of favour with one employer may be well-liked and seen as productive by another.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, over the past three years, the spotlight has been on workplace safety and health (WSH), ever since the COVID-19 pandemic caused a spike in the number of workplace fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This was only possible through the collective efforts of the tripartite partners and buy-in from both workers and supervisors on the ground to engender safer work environments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we cannot rest on our laurels, as it only takes a momentary lapse and fatalities will spike again.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How does MOM intend to build on this positive trend to ensure safer and healthier workplaces moving forward?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MOM share how are the respective sectors doing in terms of major workplace injuries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Has this move been effective, and can MOM consider extending this to other high-risk sectors?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, I hope that MOM will consider my repeated calls for there to be a mandatory WSH representative in every company, regardless of size and industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: WSH must be a foremost concern and priority in every company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Uplifting our lower-wage workers is a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Besides employers, consumers and service buyers in third-party contract models, such as those seen in the security and cleaning sectors, everyone must unite in support of lower-wage workers, actively renegotiating contracts and endorsing companies with the PW Mark.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, service providers have continued to cite difficulties in renegotiating longer-tail contracts without fear of future consequences, such as unfair debarment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some others share that contracts are renegotiated with the downgrading of worker skillsets to avoid paying the higher PWM wages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: What more can the Ministry do to further educate the service buyers and their procurement managers on PWM best practices?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Will there be better protections for service providers facing unfair and unsustainable contract negotiations due to PWM introductions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, the well-being of our lower-wage workers is critical to a fair and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Therefore, I would like to commend the efforts taken to uplift their wages and working conditions through the PWM.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Minister share an update on the progress of the PWM expansion across different sectors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Are we on track to achieve the intended outcomes, particularly in ensuring lower-wage workers receive liveable wages that reflect their contributions in this inflationary environment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Is there a plan to review and potentially further raise the LQS to benefit a larger pool of lower-wage workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: While Government policies play a vital role, collective action is key to truly uplifting lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In this regard, I would like to highlight two important stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Investing in upskilling and training lower-wage workers not only increases their productivity and employability but also empowers them to access higher-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Ministry explore further initiatives with relevant agencies to incentivise upskilling programmes for lower-wage workers across more sectors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Supporting businesses that have attained the PW Mark showcases our commitment to ethical and responsible consumption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can we partner with MTI to raise public awareness about the PW Mark and encourage conscious consumer choices that reward good practices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, we have made progress in uplifting wages of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What will be the percentage of workers who will benefit from WIS with the higher qualifying cap?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What is the target of lower-wage workers that the Ministry would like to provide support for?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The support of consumers and employers are integral in this success.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, in light of the recent adjustments to the LQS, it is evident that Singapore remains steadfast in its commitment to ensuring fair wages for local workers while maintaining effective quota controls.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst LQS will help workers, some employers have raised concerns over the upcoming increase in LQS, noting that it elevates business costs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, could MOM share how it will work with employers to ensure that the increase in LQS is bearable and not too onerous for them?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In this context, I would like to enquire about MOM's comprehensive strategy for implementing these measures effectively and ensuring that they reach a broader spectrum of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Additionally, could Minister elaborate on initiatives aimed at encouraging consumer support, such as the PW Mark, and strategies for fostering employer investment in upskilling low-wage workers to enhance their earning potential and overall well-being?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.57 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) MPs and others who have deep interests in MOM's work and spoken in support of our workers and our employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is one of the lowest among OECD countries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Real income fell slightly last year due to higher inflation, similar to what many other countries also experienced.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our recent surveys indicate an improvement in hiring and wage growth expectations from employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nevertheless, the risks of near-term headwinds remain, and this will weigh on our labour market in the year ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond the near-term headwinds, we will continue to face tight labour market constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have to confront a slowing local workforce growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the next decade, it will become harder for us to sustain high economic growth primarily from workforce growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many people have asked me what keeps me awake at night.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, keeping our competitive edge is what we should all be concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we do not succeed in sustaining our productivity in the next 10 years, my worry is that we will suffer real declines in economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses and talent will find Singapore less attractive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As a result, we will create fewer good jobs for Singaporeans and incomes will stagnate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: You have seen this story play out in other mature economies, whether in Europe, Asia or elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, Singapore has a chance to write a different story.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the accelerating pace of transformation, there will be more opportunities in new areas, like the green economy and AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Edward Chia asked about how we plan to improve the productivity and competitiveness of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I could not agree with him more that maximising our human capital is key.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means improving the skills profile of both the local and the foreign workforce and ensuring that our employers put these skills to the fullest use.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As our economy transforms, we must also channel more workers to the more productive areas of the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have to rally and unite our employers and workers towards achieving a new Forward SG social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In my MTI speech, I spoke about how the Government will support businesses in unlocking resource constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will build on this in my MOM speech by sharing how the Government will work hand-in-hand with workers and employers for a brighter future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our priorities for this year are centred on three themes: strengthening you, uplifting you and caring for you.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our first focus is to "strengthen you", by helping businesses become more productive and helping workers to take on better jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will provide an update on our efforts to spur business transformation through our foreign workforce policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also help employers strengthen the capabilities of their workforce and empower our local workers to take charge of their career health and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our second focus is to "uplift you", to ensure no one is left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As announced at Budget 2024, we will roll out the Majulah Package to support our "young seniors", who are currently in their 50s and early 60s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will recap the measures to provide greater assurance for our seniors who may be more vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad will elaborate on how our tripartite partners work hand-in-hand to uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our third focus is to "care for you", by fostering more inclusive and fair workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will empower senior workers to continue working, if they wish to, by raising our retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will provide more details, and she will also be giving updates on other workplace policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will continue working closely with our tripartite partners on all three focus areas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On this note, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to President Sister K Thanaletchmi, Secretary-General Brother Ng Chee Meng, immediate past president Sister Mary Liew from the NTUC, Brother Dr Robert Yap, President of SNEF and to all of our sisters and brothers in NTUC and SNEF for their strong support in the past year and the years ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will first share our approach to spur business transformation through our foreign workforce policies, before outlining our efforts to empower our local workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As an open economy, we will need to welcome global talent to compete on the world stage.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as a small country, we cannot increase the number of foreign workers indefinitely due to resource constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have to, therefore, be very selective about the quality of foreign workers that we take in and ensure that they are deployed in the more productive areas of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, with this in mind, we introduced major changes to our Work Pass framework over the past two years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is a highly selective pass and is aimed at facilitating the recruitment of top global talent who possess valuable networks, as well as deep skills and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In an era where talent is scarce, businesses follow talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our ONE Pass holders are the proverbial "rainmakers".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While they are not large in numbers, they are the creators of opportunities and they generate good jobs in their respective fields.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have received good interest in the ONE Pass.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Phil Inagaki is the managing director of Xora Innovation, an early stage, deep-tech investment platform of Temasek.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Before he assumed his current position, he founded and raised US$120 million in funding across five startups in businesses and industries, such as AI, clean energy and semiconductors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He helps our local startups translate scientific breakthroughs into commercial successes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The ONE Pass is also targeted at talents in areas, such as sports, arts and academia.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Assoc Prof Marco Tomamichel from the National University of Singapore (NUS) is an example of academic talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: His work focuses on quantum cryptography, which allows sensitive information to be encrypted and decrypted securely.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our young local Singaporeans have also benefited from attending his many courses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In 2022, I announced the Complementarity Assessment framework (COMPASS).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It assesses EP candidates more holistically, based on individual and firm-related attributes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This has been implemented in September last year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses, as well as HR professionals, have welcomed the introduction of COMPASS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The transparent criteria provided clarity for their manpower planning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the enhanced Self-Assessment Tool, businesses can see how their potential applicants fare on COMPASS before submitting their application.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If their candidates cannot pass COMPASS, businesses will know precisely why and what they need to do to pass.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To ensure that the quality of our foreign workforce improves in tandem with our local workforce, I have said previously that the minimum costs of hiring for S Pass and EP holders would be pegged to the top one-third of our local associate professionals and technicians (APTs) and professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By regularly updating the qualifying salaries based on the set wage benchmarks, we ensure a level-playing field for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the S Pass, we had previously announced a three-step increase in the S Pass qualifying salary and levy, with the next step taking place in 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, there will be no adjustment to the S Pass qualifying salary and levy this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The EP qualifying salary will also continue to increase progressively with age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM has heard the concerns from the various trade associations and chambers, such as the Singapore Business Federation, on rising costs of manpower and constraints in hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means that firms with existing EP holders have a longer runway, potentially up to 2028, to manage the impact of these changes and prepare their hiring plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we continue to attract top talent to grow our economy, our Work Pass framework needs to be strengthened to ensure that firms develop their local workforce and treat locals fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Patrick Tay asked how our EP framework and Fair Consideration Framework will help to achieve this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Under COMPASS, firms with a lower local PMET share relative to their sector will score fewer points on the firm-level criteria, making it harder to pass COMPASS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These firms are, hence, incentivised to improve their local PMET share.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP has been engaging and supporting firms that score poorly on firm-related attributes under COMPASS to help them improve their workforce profile and adjust to COMPASS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More than 440 firms have attended TAFEP's workshops over the past year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Firms with unfair hiring practices will still be taken to task under the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) and under the Workplace Fairness Legislation in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Desmond Choo asked about the effectiveness of the SOL in easing skills shortages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The list was designed to award bonus points on COMPASS to EP applicants filling acute occupational shortages in areas of strategic importance for the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As COMPASS was only implemented in September 2023, my update is therefore based on very preliminary data.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, the SOL is very helpful in ensuring that COMPASS does not hinder business growth because of the shortage of skills locally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As we transform our economy, some sectors in the green economy and agritech will inevitably have shortages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is especially so as these sectors are still nascent and we are pivoting to anchor them here along with the talents needed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we partner agencies in recruiting them here, we are also contemporaneously investing in developing our local talents for these jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Mr Singh's question on how MOM works with agencies to develop the local pipeline in areas of skills shortages, we are doing this systematically.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As part of the process for evaluating occupations for the SOL, MOM considers sector agencies' commitments to develop the local pipeline to address shortages in the medium-term in addition to the extent of the skills shortage.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We evaluate the progress on these commitments when we refresh the list every three years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Work Permit holders are also a critical part of our labour force.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many support essential services that local workers do not want to do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Mark Lee suggested re-evaluating the foreign worker quotas for foreign manpower for services sub-sectors facing manpower challenges, for specific job roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Edward Chia supported granting additional foreign worker quotas to firms upon commitments to human capital improvements and training for local workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the other hand, our fellow MP, Mr Sharael Taha, asked about how the Government intends to manage the inflow of Work Permit holders, given our resource constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is therefore the tension that we grapple with constantly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Mr Lee and Mr Chia's concerns on whether employers have sufficient manpower, the overall numbers speak for themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But nevertheless, let me still respond to their specific suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On Mr Lee's suggestion, we already provide targeted flexibility for some essential job roles with limited automation and localisation potential.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to review the areas where more flexibility may be required.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, there is a limit as to how much further we can differentiate to more granular job areas within the services sub-sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are also practical challenges as job roles today can be very fluid and firms can circumvent our rules by declaring a business activity or job role in an area with more generous quota.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On Mr Chia's suggestion, training can take many different forms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, workplace learning, such as on-the-job training, can help employers better manage the challenges around sending staff for external courses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It would not be viable for us to give additional quota to every single company that invests in training of their local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It can also be counter-productive, as the availability of cheaper foreign labour reduces the incentive for employers to re-design jobs and reskill their workers for greater productivity gains.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, we support firms in developing their local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will provide greater clarity in the next segment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong has emphasised, transformation is the only way that Singapore can achieve productivity-driven growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our Work Permit framework will therefore need to evolve to spur business.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The overall direction is clear; we need to improve the quality of our Work Permit holders and manage overall numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To this end, as announced at MTI’s COS on Friday, we will be making changes to the foreign workforce policies in the marine shipyard sector as a first step.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the higher-skilled R1 Work Permit holders, the levy will be increased by a smaller amount of $50, from $300 to $350.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Mark Lee also asked for an update on the Manpower for Strategic Economic Priorities Scheme (M-SEP).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: M-SEP provides additional time-bound Work Permit and S Pass quota to firms that contribute to Singapore's economic strategic priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Firms from sectors, such as construction, manufacturing and retail, have benefited from M-SEP since its inception a year ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will take in Mr Lee's suggestion as we finetune the scheme, alongside industry feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Forward SG Report has identified career agility and resilience as an important focus in our refreshed social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We encourage workers to take charge of their own career health because in this age of change and disruptions, they should have better awareness of what their career prospects are, keep their skills relevant, stay on top of the competition and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Liang Eng Hwa have asked about how the Government will work with employers, workers and intermediaries to adopt a collective mindset of building career health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan also asked about our plans to develop a future-ready workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will need a whole-of-society effort involving workers, employers and labour market intermediaries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will start with how we are supporting employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers that support the career health of their workers will be able to better attract and retain talent, tapping on adjacent talent pools to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With an agile workforce, employers will be able to quickly pivot to new opportunities in a more complex and a more uncertain economic environment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To help employers respond and plan for business transformation, the Government has launched the Jobs Transformation Maps (JTMs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A total of 16 JTMs have been completed, covering some 1.5 million resident workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will progressively launch four more in new growth areas, such as generative AI and sustainable finance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These JTMs will help employers better understand how to redesign jobs and how to reskill workers for new jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, reskilling workers for new roles can be costly upfront, and employers bear the risk that some workers may not adjust well to the demands of the new jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, WSG offers the CCPs, to co-share costs with employers who reskill new hires or existing workers for new or enhanced job roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Between 2017 and 2023, over 7,300 employers and 47,000 workers have benefitted from the CCPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One such worker who benefitted was Mr Poh Teck Hian.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the support of WSG, he secured a senior project manager position with MDesign Solutions Pte Ltd, which is a precision engineering firm.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: His employer enrolled him in the CCP for Advanced Manufacturing Engineer to enhance his skills in robotics and electronic firmware.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He is performing well in his new role, leveraging on his past engineering experience and the new skills he has picked up from the CCP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we will increase the salary support caps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will similarly increase the monthly training allowance cap for attachments under the CCPs, from $4,000 to $5,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also expand CCP for existing workers within the company.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, CCPs can only be used to reskill existing workers in jobs that are at risk of redundancy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Going forward, we will support employers who are proactively reskilling existing workers to take on new growth job roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On Mr Tay's suggestion to expand the range of CCPs, WSG will continue to review the programme offerings in consultation with the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I would urge and encourage all employers to get in touch with WSG to explore how they can tap on the CCP to meet their talent needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are supporting NTUC to set up more CTCs to work hand-in-hand with company management to drive business and workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are working with NTUC, SNEF and other TACs in the financial services, ICT, retail and precision engineering sectors to implement structured career guidance workshops.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will equip line managers and HR with capabilities to support their workers in developing career development plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This AfA, led by Dr Bicky Bhangu from SNEF and Ms Aileen Tan, a HR master professional, is working with progressive businesses and TAC leaders to develop practical solutions to support skills-based hiring and workforce agility.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As employers transform their businesses and raise productivity, workers will benefit from more meaningful jobs and improved wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers must also be motivated to better plan for their own careers, pick up relevant skills and venture beyond their comfort zone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Business leaders have consistently told me that overseas experience is valuable for career progression and, in particular, for corporate leadership positions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To support Singaporeans to venture overseas and progress in their careers, the Government will work with businesses to expand overseas opportunities for PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry announced that the Government will introduce the Global Business Leaders Programme (GBLP) to support businesses that send their Singaporean workers with leadership potential on overseas postings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The GBLP adds to the existing range of leadership development programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To complement these leadership development programmes, WSG will launch a new Overseas Markets Immersion Programme (OMIP).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The OMIP aims to encourage businesses with overseas expansion plans to send employees with little to no overseas market experience for overseas postings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employees will benefit from reskilling through on-the-job, in-market training in global or regional roles offering good prospects, whether in technology, business development or beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our businesses will also be better positioned to expand and to compete in overseas markets, with a strong globally oriented team.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The OMIP will provide financial support to the companies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More details on the GBLP and OMIP will be announced in the next few months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To take advantage of programmes like the CCPs, GBLP or OMIP, workers will need to be better equipped to make informed training and career decisions and longer-term career plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why we launched the CareersFinder feature on the MyCareersFuture portal last year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: CareersFinder harnesses data and AI to help Singaporeans explore pathways to acquiring new skills and reach their career goals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The early signs are encouraging as we find these workers do go on to broaden their horizons by applying for jobs across a wider range of occupations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Taylor Swift aptly puts it from her hit song titled, "You belong with me", "Tell me about your dreams, I think I know where you belong".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will empower Singaporeans to seize their dream career opportunities by helping them take charge of their career health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are looking at ways to enable workers to better signal their skills to employers or potential hirers, so that they are better recognised and rewarded.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will strengthen the linkage between skills acquisition and career progression.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also want to make career guidance, both in-person and through AI-enabled digital platforms, more accessible to even more Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about how we intend to report on the success of our initiatives to improve employment outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Real wages have grown over the longer-term, underpinned by sustained productivity growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Liang Eng Hwa have asked for an update on the financial support scheme for involuntarily unemployed jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As the Deputy Prime Minister said, we will announce the scheme later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have considered feedback and suggestions from tripartite partners and the public, including recommendations from the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce in 2021 and the Citizens' Panel on Employment Resilience in 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are close to finalising the scheme parameters, and I want to assure the House that we have, indeed, looked at best practices around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, our payouts will be conditional on jobseekers making the effort to actively search for a job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will avoid the unintended consequences faced by other countries in implementing similar schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Gerald Giam asked if we could better recognise the contributions of tradespeople and make skilled trades more attractive for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned again in the Forward SG report, the Government will work with the Labour Movement, industry and communities of tradespeople to develop and testbed initiatives to professionalise skilled trades, such as developing structured training and career pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will study interventions for electricians first, with a view to scaling to more occupations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On Mr Pritam Singh's proposal to legislate retrenchment benefit, including for those in "hands" and "heart" roles, we have no plans to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is consistent with our stance on retrenchment benefit for all employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Legally mandating retrenchment benefit will affect the viability of businesses which are already in financial difficulty and put existing employees at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Additionally, the businesses that can afford to pay more will default to the legislated minimum.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am going to move to the next section on "uplifting you" and how we ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Securing better jobs during an individual's working years empowers and enables you to be financially secure when you retire.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to assure Singaporeans that as long as you work and contribute consistently to CPF, you will be able to meet your basic retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, it is not as alarming as what the Leader of the Opposition characterised retirement adequacy to be: a "serious and ongoing concern".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even then, the Government is committed to uplifting Singaporeans who need more help as part of our refreshed social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At Budget 2024, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a significant suite of retirement adequacy measures.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government has enhanced the Majulah Package, after it was announced at the National Day Rally last year, to support all Singaporeans born in 1973 or earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, enhancements to the WIS, SSS and the MRSS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, moves to rationalise the CPF system, in particular the closure of the Special Account (SA) and the raising of the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This infographic illustrates how every older Singaporean will benefit from our comprehensive suite of measures for retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members may also access the infographic through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since Budget 2024, there has been much discussion on the closure of the SA for CPF members aged 55 and above.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many, including Mr Desmond Choo, have asked why the Government is making this move now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The closure of the SA, together with the significant suite of measures for retirement adequacy that we will be rolling out, is part of the evolution of the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Fundamentally, the CPF system is designed to provide for members' basic retirement needs, as well as support their housing and healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With rising incomes and savings of fellow Singaporeans, stable CPF returns and trust in the CPF system, many of us would like to save more than the FRS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some hope for higher investment returns; others hope to leave a bequest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will work hard at providing stable returns appropriate for savings that can be withdrawn in the shorter term, as well as those set aside for longer term retirement needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, as the CPF system evolves, the fundamental objectives of addressing retirement, housing and healthcare needs remain, for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When CPF was first introduced in 1955, Singaporeans had little retirement savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As our economy grew, subsequent cohorts benefited from high employment rates and strong wage growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As a result, Singaporeans today can set aside more in their CPF accounts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The number of members voluntarily topping up their CPF accounts has more than doubled from 2020 to 2022, demonstrating strong trust in the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The number and proportion of CPF members with withdrawable SA balances has also increased and will continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is not consistent with the principle that only long-term savings should earn the higher long-term interest rate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the Budget Debate, Ms Foo Mee Har said that closing the SA "affects many middle-income seniors" and suggested for a "fairer option" of grandfathering the SA for existing members aged 55 and above.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Foo Mee Har's suggestion will inadvertently create a generational divide, benefiting the current generation of older Singaporeans, while disadvantaging younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those affected by the move are generally the more well-off.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Leong Mun Wai can see that closing the SA is not a move to save interest payments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These remaining 8,400 members, the less than 1% with higher balances, can transfer their CPF savings to the RA of their family members or grow them outside the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, I note Ms Foo Mee Har's support for the raising of the ERS, from three times to four times of the BRS, from 2025.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This move is, indeed, intended to help the broad middle.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Ms Hazel Poa, the ERS cap on RA balances is necessary to ensure that the CPF system continues to serve the broad majority.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These members have a few options to choose from when the SA is closed next year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, these members with the median balance of about $2,000 in the SA can retain these balances in the OA for liquidity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Compared to the SA, there will be lower interest earned, with a difference of about $3 per month, or about $30 per year at the median.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, they can choose to invest in safe instruments, such as the Singapore Government Securities through the CPF Investment Scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, they can top up their RA, up to the raised ERS, to receive higher retirement payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Chua said that interest committed to CPF LIFE "will not accrue to the CPF holder" but is pooled together for all members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CPF LIFE is an insurance scheme that addresses the risk of outliving one's savings by providing members with lifelong monthly payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This risk-pooling allows CPF members to get monthly payouts for as long as they live.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Upon a member's passing, any unused premium is refunded to the member's beneficiaries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, members need to be clear about what they are getting with their RA savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Each member will need to assess for themselves what level of retirement payouts they desire.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to highlight that CPF LIFE premium continues to earn interest, which is factored into members' CPF LIFE monthly payouts that will last as long as they live.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Business Times published an article, about a week ago, that called CPF LIFE "the best annuity in the market".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members today are allowed to opt out if they have a pension or an annuity that pays the same or higher monthly payouts for life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If Mr Louis Chua knows of any similar or better products, he, too, can apply to opt out of CPF LIFE.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is also not locking up members' savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By age 70, members are required to start drawing down on their CPF savings through retirement payouts, and this is in line with CPF's core objective of providing a lifelong retirement income.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, some members have written to me requesting to defer their payout start age to beyond 70 years old.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want members to enjoy their hard-earned monies by that age.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With all these clarifications, I trust that Members of this House and Singaporeans will better appreciate why we are closing the SA for those aged 55 and above.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, the changes announced are "very much in line with the purpose and intent of the CPF", which is for retirement, for housing and for healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not about saving costs for the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nearly all CPF members can continue to earn the higher interest rate if they choose to transfer their SA savings to their RA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Furthermore, the SA closure should also be seen alongside the other significant measures that we are making to boost the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We must evolve our CPF system while retaining its focus on serving the broad majority and providing more support to those with less.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am heartened that MPs, like Mr Neil Parekh, have expressed support for this as a step in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ultimately, we want to assure Singaporeans that the Government remains committed to uplifting those who need more support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is therefore rolling out the Majulah Package to support our "young seniors" who are currently in their 50s and early 60s.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Compared to younger Singaporeans, they have generally earned less during their working years, and they have a shorter runway to benefit from recent improvements to the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many of them are sandwiched between caring for both the young and the old in their families.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Earn and Save Bonus will cover around seven in 10 older employed Singaporean workers, who are lower- to middle-income, earning up to $6,000 per month, with more support going to those earning less.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The first Earn and Save Bonus will be credited into your CPF account in 2025, based on the work done last year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This bonus will be credited into your CPF account by the end of this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We recognise that healthcare cost is a concern for all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, all older Singaporeans will receive this by the end of this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond the Majulah Package, the Government is also enhancing existing schemes to help those who may need more support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will further enhance the WIS scheme to help our lower-wage workers build up their retirement savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will spend around $300 million more, spending a total of around $1.4 billion in 2025.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will benefit around half a million lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad will provide more details.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will update SSS to better support seniors who have less for retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, we will proceed with the next step of the increase in senior workers' CPF contribution rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate on these schemes to support older Singaporeans in his speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To address the concerns raised by Mr Desmond Choo and other Members, caregivers and homemakers who are unable to work and are, thus, ineligible to receive the Earn and Save Bonus, still benefit from the MediSave Bonus, Retirement Savings Bonus, enhanced Silver Support Scheme and the MRSS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A "young senior" who will benefit from the Majulah Package is Ms Caroline Ng.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: She is 54 years old this year, and lives with her husband and son in a 4-room flat.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Together with her sister-in-law, Ms Ng is also supporting her elderly mother-in-law.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Ng and her husband are in a sandwiched phase of life: 上有老，下有小.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Ng started her career in HR but stopped working to take care of her young son then and the elderly in her family.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As her son grew more independent, Ms Ng rejoined the workforce in 2020, with the guidance of a career coach from WSG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: She subsequently took a temporary career break and she is now looking forward to return to the workforce again.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Ng is excited about the Majulah Package because the Earn and Save Bonus and Retirement Savings Bonus can help her set aside more CPF savings as they translate into higher retirement payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, Ms Ng, her husband and elderly mother-in-law will also receive the MediSave Bonus to pay for their own healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Speaking of active ageing, another young senior who is looking forward to the Majulah Package is Mdm Norizan.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: She is 59 years old this year and works in the F&B industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that the Earn and Save Bonus will encourage many more older Singaporeans, like Mdm Norizan to continue working, if they can and if they wish to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Hazel Poa suggested to improve flexibility and returns on CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CPF balances earn returns pegged to market instruments of comparable risk and duration, but the investment risk is entirely borne by the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, I would like to remind members that higher returns come with higher risk.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Louis Chua called on the Government to implement the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the benefit of hindsight on historical returns these few years, it is easy to comment on what should have been done.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Although the current outlook for 2024 has improved, there is still considerable uncertainty, with risks tilted to the downside.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: No one can be sure how the markets will move.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, as per Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's and my previous explanations to Mr Louis Chua, it is not straightforward to introduce the LRIS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The LRIS will introduce a new element of risk for retirees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Regardless, we will continue to study the LRIS proposal, and we will work on making the CPF system even better for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Louis Chua talked about the interest rate peg for the OA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is aware that the OA interest rate has remained relatively stable, while yields of market instruments of comparable risk and duration have increased.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to review our CPF interest rates periodically to ensure their relevance in the prevailing operating environment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Ong Hua Han suggested expanding the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) to cover more members with pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The HPS today already covers members with pre-existing health conditions, including PwDs, if they are assessed to be generally in good health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nevertheless, we are reviewing ways to further expand the coverage of the HPS, but we also have to take into consideration the affordability of premiums across the wider group.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, taken together, the significant suite of measures that I have talked about will ensure that the CPF system retains its focus on serving the broad majority, while uplifting those who need more support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to assure Singaporeans that you can retire with peace of mind in your golden years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Moving on to my final point on "caring for you".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to provide all Singaporeans with opportunities to participate in our transformation journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government will work hand-in-hand with employers and workers to build more inclusive and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For seniors who wish to continue working, our tripartite partners have agreed in 2019 to increase the retirement and re-employment ages to 65 and 70 by 2030.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We successfully made one round of increase in July 2022.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, I am pleased to announce that we have reached a tripartite agreement to implement the next round of increase to the retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will share more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will also introduce two important Bills in Parliament this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we recognise the importance of fair workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is why the Government accepted the recommendation by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness to introduce a new Workplace Fairness Legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will further strengthen protections against discrimination and provide greater assurance to workers who wish to report grievances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We note Ms He Ting Ru's views and we look forward to discussing this Bill robustly in the House in time to come.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, we will update our regulatory frameworks to strengthen protections for our platform workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will include areas, such as housing, retirement adequacy, work injury compensation and representation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether you are a youth starting your career, a mid-career worker looking at the next steps or a senior in your golden years, the Government will walk every step with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For youths, we will empower you to plan out your careers and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For mid-career workers, we will equip you with the means to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes replenishing your skills to stay ahead and reskilling support if you want a career change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For seniors approaching retirement, you will be able to meet your basic retirement needs as long as you have contributed consistently to your CPF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to strengthen support for those who may need more help along the way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workers can also look forward to more inclusive and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These measures support a refreshed social compact to take us forward together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are aware that some of our policy measures announced today will have an impact on business costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, I must emphasise – and I want to seek everyone's support, understanding and indulgence – that a significant part of the cost increase is going towards uplifting our local lower-wage workers and improving the livelihoods of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, when we also look at the profitability of our businesses, we still remain competitive compared to other economies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, I hope that our employers can support us and carry the shared burden and responsibility of our refreshed social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the Labour Movement, employers, workers and Government working hand-in-hand, I am confident that we will build a better future together!

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, let me now say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the past year, I have participated in many conversations under the Forward SG exercise and heard the aspirations of Singaporeans regarding employment and retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM deeply understands and pays close attention to the anxieties and aspirations of Singaporeans for the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Regardless of your age group and challenges you face, we will walk with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you are looking to switch jobs, the CareersFinder feature on the MyCareersFuture website can recommend suitable jobs and training courses to help you better plan your career.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers can also tap on the CCPs to hire new talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, the Government will gradually raise the retirement and re-employment ages and increase the CPF contribution rates for senior workers to help you accumulate more CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For vulnerable groups and retirees who need more support, we will enhance the Silver Support Scheme and the MRSS to strengthen your financial security in retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At different stages in life, we all have different pursuits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In our youth, we are full of ambition, believing that we have innate talents and hoping to build a grand career.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In our prime, we continue to improve and challenge ourselves, aiming to reach new heights in our careers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In our golden years, we hope to enjoy a peaceful retirement and, at the same time, contribute our wisdom to guide the next generation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the saying goes, the younger generation will surpass the older generation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We hope that our next generation can make greater contributions to society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As we journey towards our goals, setbacks are inevitable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the lows of our lives, we all hope to have close friends by our side, sharing our joys and sorrows and helping us through the difficult times.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This reminds me of a well-known song by Wakin Chau, "Friends": "Friends never feel lonely, a true friend will understand." The Government and our tripartite partners will stand shoulder to shoulder with employers, workers and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As long as we can unite and support each other, we can certainly progress towards a brighter future.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will take the clarifications at the end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Members may also access the handout through the SG PARL MP Mobile App.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, tripartism is at the centre of Singapore's approach to uplifting lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the years, the Government has worked closely together with employers and unions to support the advancement of lower-wage workers in a sustainable manner so that everyone can enjoy the fruits of Singapore's growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Progressive Wages and Workfare are a big part of our collective efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, the PWM provides for career and training progression pathways for lower-wage workers in sectors and occupations with many of such workers, ensuring that wages rise sustainably.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Members may refer to the info sheet for PWM for the ladders and trajectories and their salaries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Second, for the remaining sectors and occupations, local workers must still be paid at least the LQS, if their employers hire foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government provides employers with transitional co-funding of wage increases for lower-wage workers, through the PWCS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Through Workfare, the Government further supplements the incomes of lower-wage workers to help them to save more for retirement and support them for upskilling through training.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This year is a momentous milestone in Singapore's journey of uplifting lower-wage workers, as it marks the 10th anniversary of our first PWM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with other tripartite efforts, PWMs have supported lower-wage workers in seeing sustained and meaningful wage growth over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the past two years, we have expanded Progressive Wages to cover even more lower-wage workers, and this follows the release of recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers in 2021.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Fahmi Aliman asked about the progress of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is more than five times the coverage in 2020.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have expanded quite significantly since 2020.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, over 105,000 lower-wage workers are covered by the LQS requirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our suite of Progressive Wage moves – comprising PWMs, LQS and the Progressive Wage Mark accreditation scheme – now benefit up to nine in 10 of full-time lower-wage workers today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In a tight labour market, lower-wage workers who are not directly covered by Progressive Wages should also see increases in their wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Fahimi Aliman and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about how we will build upon existing efforts to uplift lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A key step that we will take is to raise the LQS threshold.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The LQS threshold ensures that locals are employed meaningfully, rather than on token salaries for firms to access foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We regularly review the LQS threshold to keep pace with rising local wages and maintain the effectiveness of our foreign workforce controls.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government last updated the LQS threshold in 2020 before the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognised that firms needed time to comply with the new LQS requirement, which came into effect in September 2022.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, local wages have increased with our recovery from the pandemic and we are thus adjusting the LQS threshold.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Correspondingly, foreign worker quota computation will be adjusted.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To be counted as one local workforce count (LWC) for the purpose of foreign worker quota for firms – or one LWC – the local worker will need to be paid at least $1,600.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For firms hiring part-time workers, locals who earn at least half the LQS are counted as half an LWC.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With the LQS increase, such locals have to be paid at least $800, up from $700 today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These changes will be implemented on 1 July 2024.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the Government’s part, we will continue providing lower-wage workers with additional support through Workfare, to complement our Progressive Wage efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare comprises two key pillars: WIS, and the Workfare Skills Support Scheme (WSS).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the years, the Government has steadily strengthened our Workfare support for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As announced by the Deputy Prime Minister at Budget, the Government will further enhance Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Sharael Taha would be pleased to note that this ensures Workfare continues to help workers in the bottom 20th income percentiles, with some support for those slightly above.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will increase the maximum payment to $4,900 per year, up from $4,200.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Those aged 60 and above will benefit from this highest payment tier for Workfare, as well as all PwDs regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Payments for all other qualifying age groups will also be increased.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Those aged 30 to 34 will receive a maximum payment of $2,450 per year; those aged 35 to 44 will receive a maximum payment of $3,500 per year; and those aged 45 to 59 will receive a maximum payment of $4,200 per year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These enhancements will benefit around half a million lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In total, WIS payments will increase to $1.4 billion in 2025, up from $1.1 billion last year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Another key step that the Government will take is ensuring employees are aware of the Progressive Wages they are eligible for.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We thus launched the Progressive Wage Portal (PW Portal), earlier in January.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Even as we support our lower-wage workers, we also understand and are aware that employers face uncertain economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They have continued paying their lower-wage workers good wages and upskilled them, even for those not on PWM, and despite challenging economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We need to be mindful of the impact of Progressive Wages on employers in the short run.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We should ensure that as we uplift lower-wage workers, we do not inadvertently harm workers’ prospects or risk widespread job losses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, in 2022, the Government introduced PWCS to co-fund wage increases that employers give their lower-earning employees.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PWCS provides transitional support for employers to adjust to new PWM and LQS requirements, and encourages voluntary wage increases for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Through PWCS, the Government has supported meaningful wage increases for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Sharael Taha’s query, the Government will indeed continue providing transitional support to employers through PWCS over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As outlined by the Deputy Prime Minister at the Budget, the Government will further enhance PWCS this year to help employers cope with PWM and LQS increases amid a more challenging economic environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, we will increase the Government’s co-funding for wage increases given in 2024.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This builds on earlier enhancements in 2022 and 2023 at 75% co-funding.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This includes workers who are not covered by any PWM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With this enhancement, PWCS will continue to support increases of wages up to $3,000 beyond 2024.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Collectively, both enhancements will offset a significant proportion of immediate cost pressures on employers arising from our efforts to uplift lower-wage workers and mitigate cost transfer to consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To provide for these enhancements, the Deputy Prime Minister has announced a top-up of $1 billion to the PWCS Fund.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This brings the total PWCS budget to $6.2 billion.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with the increased Workfare payments of up to $1.4 billion per year – $6.2 billion for PWCS and $1.4 billion per year in Workfare payments – I think that is quite significant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope Members can see that the Government has committed and invested significant resources into strengthening and supporting our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, the Government cannot single-handedly drive the growth of lower-wage workers’ incomes, nor can we co-fund wage increases given to lower-wage workers indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Mr Edward Chia, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Sharael Taha said, uplifting lower-wage workers is a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers need to improve their skills, so they can be as productive as they can be in their jobs, as their wages rises.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Lower-wage workers tend to be in frontline roles, where their productivity growth is heavily dependent on how the firms and industries that they work in operate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This means that transformation must also take place at the firm- and industry-level, as Mr Edward Chia said, so that we can narrow the wage gap in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Industries must therefore accelerate the pace of their transformation journeys, taking guidance from ITMs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers must accelerate their individual business transformation plans and drive productivity gains within their firms, through better technology and processes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers can find support through Government schemes, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers can also consider working with NTUC to set up CTCs and tap on the NTUC CTC grant to transform businesses, redesign jobs and improve work prospects for their employees.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Service buyers have a role to play too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Where there is a need to renegotiate existing contracts for compliance with Progressive Wages, service buyers and service providers should work together to come to a mutually agreeable solution.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Above all, service buyers should embrace outcome-based contracting, which focuses on specifying clear and deliverable outcomes, rather than the exact number of workers for individual tasks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This allows service providers to deliver quality services using less manpower and enables employers to pay higher wages to their lower-wage workers using productivity as a tool.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Last but not least, consumers can make their choices count, by purchasing from businesses accredited with the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, over 4,400 businesses are PW Mark-accredited, and more are coming onboard each day.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Supporting PW Mark businesses means supporting lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Both you and I can make our purchase matter and help uplift lower-wage workers more sustainably.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, I move on to HR and strengthening HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: HR is a key enabler for workforce and business success, and MOM remains committed to strengthening employers’ HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Edward Chia asked how MOM is empowering employers to adopt job redesign.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
