text: WSG, in collaboration with IHRP, launched the Job Redesign Centre of Excellence (JRCoE) last November.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: JRCoE serves as a one-stop centre to equip enterprises with capabilities to transform their business and workforce through job redesign.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Around 20 TACs have pledged support for the JRCoE and will be encouraging their member companies to incorporate job redesign in HR practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is the first time it has fallen below one per 100,000 workers, aside from 2020 when COVID-19 disrupted work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Only four OECD countries have achieved this consistently – the UK, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If we can sustain this, this puts us among the top performers of WSH in the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have achieved this milestone five years ahead of target year 2028 because of the Government’s close partnership with employers and workers, and certainly with the help of the labour movement as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The key challenge moving forward – and our goal has to be this – is to sustain the rate at below one.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This requires all stakeholders to press on with our collective efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Business leaders must continue to reinforce a strong and pervasive culture of workplace safety excellence, and invest in WSH technologies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Unions must advocate for safe, healthy workplaces and working conditions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the ground, proper risk assessment and management must be done.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers must continue to follow safety protocols, speak up to improve WSH practices, and call out safety risks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On our part, the Government will continue to push out the Safety Accountability, Focus and Empowerment (SAFE) measures announced last May, and strengthen WSH ownership of employers and workers through programmes and resources.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will continue to closely monitor sectoral WSH performance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Key findings for 2023 will be shared in the WSH National Statistics Report scheduled for release by this April.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Through our collective efforts and vigilance, I believe we can sustain our achievement in 2023 for the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked about the compensation under WICA.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Insurers have to adhere to claims, processing standards and guidelines, including how compensation is computed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The median time for designated insurers to process a WIC claim is about six months, and processing time varies depending on the complexity of the case.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, just this February, MOM announced increases to the WICA compensation limits to keep pace with wage growth and rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These changes will be implemented from November 2025.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will continue reviewing WICA regularly to ensure that workers have access to expeditious and fair compensation in case of work injury.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is committed to working hand-in-hand with employers, service buyers, consumers and workers themselves, to build a safer and more inclusive workplace.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must continue to progress together as one people to ensure that no worker is left behind and that all workers have the opportunity to achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to recap some of MOM’s efforts in Malay, please. :   Over the years, the Government has worked closely together with employers and NTUC unions to support the advancement of lower-wage workers in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with other tripartite efforts, PWMs have supported lower-wage workers in seeing meaningful wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PWM workers, in particular, have seen strong wage outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Here, I recall the situation of workers, like Ms Sivamani Taigrajan.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As a new auxiliary security officer when she started working in 2005, Ms Sivamani earned a monthly salary of $800.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Throughout her nearly 20-year career in the security industry, Ms Sivamani has continued to upskill and take on greater and new responsibilities, guided by the PWM framework for the security industry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Now as a security supervisor, Ms Sivamani earns a monthly salary of $3,250, which is a significant progress from her initial monthly salary of $800.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This demonstrates the effectiveness of the PWM in supporting meaningful wage increases for our workers, as they enhance their skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is more than five times the previous PWM coverage in 2020.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Under the PWM, workers can receive annual wage increases and expect to earn at least the relevant PWM salary.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, cleaners will see their pay rise to at least $2,420 per month by 2028.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, over 105,000 lower-wage workers are covered by the LQS requirement, where firms employing foreign manpower must pay all their local workers at least the LQS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with the PW Mark accreditation scheme, our suite of Progressive Wage measures, comprising the PWMs, LQS and the PW Mark, now benefit nine in 10 of full-time lower-wage workers today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is strengthening our efforts to raise the salaries and well-being of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Second, we will enhance Workfare to further strengthen our support for lower-wage workers to help them to save more for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the years to come, I would like to give my assurance to Members in this Chamber that the Government will continue to work together with employers and NTUC to ensure that everyone advances and enjoy the fruits of Singapore’s growth together, as one, through the good times and the bad times.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now speak more about MOM's measures to uplift Singaporeans and workers who may be more vulnerable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This includes our efforts to boost retirement adequacy of our seniors and improve protections for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will also cover our ongoing efforts to support the well-being of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These generations have generally earned less over their lifetime and had a shorter runway to benefit from the improvements to our CPF system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We want to assure Singaporeans that as long as one works and contributes consistently to CPF, you will be able to meet your retirement needs through CPF payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But what about those who are not able to work and contribute consistently to their CPF accounts?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some may accumulate less CPF savings due to low wages during their working years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Others may not work consistently due to caregiving responsibilities or disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Yip Hon Weng and other MPs at the Budget Debate have rightly pointed out, we will also need to boost the retirement adequacy of these groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Families, employers and the community play a key role in supporting our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is an important part of our social compact and the Government will continue to encourage and support this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will enhance our support in the following ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we will continue to encourage family, employers and the community to support our seniors with lower retirement savings by enhancing the MRSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, we will also enhance the Silver Support Scheme for seniors who had low incomes during their working years and have less family support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced at Budget, we are committed to raising the CPF contribution rates for senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have implemented the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers' recommendation to increase the CPF contribution rates for senior workers since 2022 and will continue to do so in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will continue to support employers with the CPF Transition Offset for the first year of implementation of this increase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to also thank our tripartite partners for their continued support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These recommendations are necessary so that our senior workers can enter retirement with more confidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even with the increase in senior workers' CPF contribution rates, some seniors may still face challenges in accumulating their CPF savings for retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We want to supplement efforts by families, employers and the community to help these seniors to save more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2021, the Government introduced MRSS as a pilot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under MRSS, the Government provides a dollar-for-dollar matching grant on cash top-ups made to the Retirement Account of eligible senior Singapore Citizens aged between 55 and 70 with lower retirement savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The matching grant is capped at $600 per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Anyone can make these top-ups – individuals themselves, family members, employers and the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The positive response for MRSS showed that financially savvy members have chosen to make top-ups to loved ones' CPF accounts as a way of growing their retirement savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Thus, as Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced in his Budget speech, we will continue the scheme beyond the pilot and enhance the scheme in two ways from 2025 onwards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, the MRSS will be extended beyond the current age cap of 70.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I am glad that Ms Hazel Poa agrees with this move.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The number of Singaporeans eligible for the enhanced MRSS will thus double to about 800,000 per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A $20,000 cap will apply over an eligible member's lifetime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, an eligible senior who receives annual cash top-ups of $2,000 for 10 years can see his retirement savings increase by about $48,000, which translates to about a $260 increase in his lifelong monthly CPF payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As our seniors enter their golden years, many of us want to better support them in old age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, many of us regularly give them cash allowances to cover their daily expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I would urge more Singaporeans to consider topping up their parents' CPF, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This can be done in regular, small amounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: She has been giving her parents monthly cash allowance since she started working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On top of that, Ms Tay has a GIRO arrangement with the CPF Board since 2018 to make monthly cash top-ups into her parents' Retirement Accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Her mother is also eligible for the MRSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, when the MRSS was introduced in 2021, her mother benefited from the dollar-for-dollar matching of her GIRO top-ups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Tay said that MRSS is a good initiative to get Singaporeans to top up their parents' Retirement Account and earn the risk-free CPF interest rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the upcoming enhancements to the MRSS to increase the annual matching grant quantum, Ms Tay intends to also increase her cash top-ups so that she can help to increase her parents' monthly retirement payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those who choose to follow in Ms Tay's footsteps, the Government will augment your efforts by providing the MRSS matching grant to eligible seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The community can also use the MRSS to support those who need more help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A good example is Fei Yue Community Services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2021 and 2022, they identified seniors living alone in rental flats in their community and worked with members of the public to raise over S$300,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The donations were credited as cash top-ups into the Retirement Accounts of over 500 senior beneficiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Another community partner of MRSS is Tsao Foundation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since 2021, Tsao Foundation has been encouraging seniors to save more for their retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Tsao Foundation provided additional cash top-ups so that the seniors under their programme receive the maximum annual matching grant from the Government when they top-up their Retirement Account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Tsao Foundation intends to further extend its campaign so that more seniors can benefit from MRSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition to the increase in senior workers' contribution rates and MRSS enhancements, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and the Minister have also shared that the Government will be enhancing the SSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The increase in SSS quarterly payments by 20% to keep pace with inflation should address Mr Yip Hon Weng's concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to review the SSS regularly to target support at seniors who need it the most while ensuring that the scheme remains fiscally sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: All in all, the enhancements to the CPF system enable a whole-of-society effort to support the retirement adequacy of our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Individuals, employers, family members and the community, all of us can do our part to fortify our social compact and build a community that is kind and cares for one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is the essence of the Forward SG Exercise led by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me now to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Through conversations with the people, we have come to understand that many Singaporeans approaching retirement age are very concerned about their retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government has introduced the Majulah Package and other new measures to enhance retrenchment adequacy to meet the basic retirement needs of elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will collaborate with families, community groups and employers to provide more assistance to vulnerable elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Anyone can make contributions to the Retirement Accounts of elderly Singaporeans, including CPF members themselves, family members, employers or even the community groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I encourage children to regularly contribute to their elderly parents' CPF accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will also provide dollar-for-dollar matching to help increase their retirement savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, their monthly payout from their CPF LIFE will increase by about $260.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will also assist elderly Singaporeans with lower CPF savings and less family support through the SSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The per capita monthly income ceiling for eligible households will also be raised, benefitting about 290,000 elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government is committed to helping elderly Singaporeans with their retirement security, allowing them to enjoy their golden years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To achieve this goal, we also need the collective effort of the whole society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Therefore, I encourage families, employers and community groups to reach out and lend a helping hand to those in need around them, so that elderly Singaporeans can have a sense of security in old age and enjoy a “springtime” retirement. : Sir, let me move on to the issue of employment protection for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Jean See asked how freelancers can be protected for workplace safety and health risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under the Workplace Safety and Health Act, service buyers have a duty to ensure the safety of contracted freelancers who work under their direction or at their work premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If a freelancer is injured at work, he or she can pursue a civil claim against the service buyer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Compensation will depend on the facts of the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For certainty of coverage, freelancers should consider personal accident insurance for their own financial protection in case of injury.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As their own boss, freelancers have control over their business model and pricing to negotiate key service terms with service buyers, such as fees and whether to include the cost of their insurance coverage within their contract pricing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will continue to work with associations to provide guidance on what businesses should do when contracting with freelancers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Jean See also raised various suggestions at the Budget Debate on how to better support freelancers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will take these suggestions from the Labour Movement into account as we review how to better protect workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond work injury compensation, the Government is also committed to ensuring that our employment regulations remain relevant and provide sufficient protection for employees, while maintaining a competitive business environment that continues to generate good jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas suggested several areas within the Employment Act for review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the meantime, I would like to assure Members, such as Mr Louis Chua and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, that the Government will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners to ensure that exploitative employment practices do not become the norm in our workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's suggestion to legislate against restraint of trade clauses for employees who are of a certain pay grade, theoretically, this sounds like an easy thing to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But in practice, the specific types of jobs that interact substantively with an employer's legitimate business interests will depend on each employer's business considerations and structures as well as other case-specific factors, such as the nature of work that the employee is engaged in at that time and the position of the employee within the organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It will not be appropriate nor feasible for tripartite partners to take a one-size-fits-all approach and prescribe exhaustively the specific circumstances in which restraint of trade clauses are reasonable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers should assess if there is a genuine need for restraint of trade clauses to protect legitimate business interests based on principles that the Courts have already previously set out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the meantime, I urge employees who believe that they have been subject to such practices to seek assistance from their unions or TAFEP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These guidelines will shape the norms of behaviour to strengthen fairness in the use of such clauses in employment contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As the Minister mentioned, we are strongly committed to strengthening Singaporeans' job prospects and career health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, we need to transform the migrant worker ecosystem and improve their well-being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through collaborations with more than 160 partners, including stakeholders like dormitory operators and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), we have made significant improvements in migrant workers' well-being in a holistic way, from their workplace concerns to housing, healthcare and their social needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And, by 2040, all regulated dormitories, including new and existing ones, will meet even higher dormitory standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These measures will strengthen public health resilience and better prepare us for future disease outbreaks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Louis Chua mentioned the need to ensure that companies are able to access adequate accommodation at reasonable standards and prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Pre-COVID-19, the number of dormitory beds available was sized to adequately meet the demand, with a healthy 90% occupancy rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: When the economy reopened after COVID-19, employers were desperate to catch up on projects that were delayed by COVID-19 and have been hiring more migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, the number of Work Permit holders in the construction, marine and process sectors is 20% higher than pre-COVID-19 days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This led to a market-induced relative shortage of dormitory beds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM has been working closely with key stakeholders to make more dormitory beds available to accommodate this growth while ensuring they meet MOM's dormitory standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since December 2022, 17,000 more dormitory beds have been added through various measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These measures have helped to alleviate pressure on the broader housing market and rental prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, the growth in the migrant worker population has outpaced the increase in dormitory supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is not sustainable to keep building migrant worker dormitories or adding more beds to house new workers, because when the catch-up projects are eventually completed and the excess workers return to their home countries, we may end up swinging to the other extreme and end up with an excess of dormitory beds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Thus, the more sustainable way forward is for employers to reduce their reliance on migrant workers by adopting productivity measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I am glad Mr Louis Chua agrees with us that this is the right thing to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is why we have the Skills Recognition Framework in place, which encourages employers to retain experienced and skilled Work Permit holders through lower levies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms He Ting Ru suggested that employers should be required to wait one month before repatriating migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Her concern is that repatriation may arise from retaliation by the employer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Should this be the case, they should approach MOM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: When migrant workers are onboarded, we inform them of their rights and avenues to seek help if they are unfairly treated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Upon notification, MOM will investigate and issue a special pass to allow the worker to remain in Singapore until investigations are completed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If employers have been found to be victimising their employees, enforcement action will be taken against the relevant employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope Ms He Ting Ru does not forget that, at times, migrant workers themselves are at fault, leading to the end of the employment relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, if a migrant domestic worker has been mistreating children in a household, I think it would not be reasonable to expect the employer to continue keeping the migrant domestic worker in the household and providing for her upkeep instead of repatriating her immediately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how we will safeguard the well-being of migrant workers and ensure that they receive fair treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As the Member has previously raised similar questions in Parliament, I will just provide a brief overview.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On food hygiene, employers and dormitory operators must only procure food from licensed food establishments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM also conducts regular inspections on dormitories to check that food delivered to the dormitories is protected from contamination until it is collected by the residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested to increase the penalties for employment kickbacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This indicates that the current caps remain sufficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have also strengthened protections for workers to encourage them to come forward early without fear of reprisal, as we will facilitate a change of employer if necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers can also report kickbacks through multiple avenues, such as our MOM hotline or to our Forward Assurance and Support Teams (FAST) team officers deployed on the ground or through the FWMOMCare app.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue working with partners to enhance programmes and events in the recreation centres to better meet migrant workers' social needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, to uplift Singaporeans, the Government has put in place measures to boost the retirement adequacy of our seniors and improve protection of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, we have continued to transform the migrant worker ecosystem by improving existing housing and healthcare needs and increasing engagements with our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to work closely with stakeholders, including our tripartite partners to implement the initiatives I have shared about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the support of the whole-of-society, I am confident that we can uplift those who are more vulnerable among us as we build a shared future together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members who have given suggestions on upholding inclusivity and fairness at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In our refreshed social compact, we want to ensure that all members of our society can participate in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Given our ageing population and slowing workforce growth, it is important that we help every worker contribute as much as they are able to, for as long as they wish.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Several Members, including Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Miss Rachel Ong, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Keith Chua, have spoken on this subject.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Retirement and Re-employment Act protects seniors from age-related dismissal before reaching the statutory retirement age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers must offer re-employment to eligible senior workers up until the statutory re-employment age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Credit goes to employers and our union leaders on the ground as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over nine in 10 senior workers who were eligible and wished to continue working were offered re-employment in 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To ensure that the next increase is implemented just as smoothly, I encourage employers to start planning early.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some will need to adjust their manpower and upskilling plans to retain their senior workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is why we are taking a stepped approach and announcing the increase early.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Come 2026, employers who have prepared well will be better placed to tap on their senior workforce to meet their business needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our employment rate for seniors aged 65 to 69 is now ranked third compared to OECD countries, increasing by almost five percentage points, from 43.8% in 2018 to 48.3% in 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Among our younger seniors aged 55 to 64, the employment rate also rose, from 66.8% to 70.0% over the same period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we can do more to support our seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As Miss Rachel Ong has highlighted, senior workers have much expertise to contribute, but some may prefer to reduce their work intensity as they age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Workplaces with FWA provisions will be better able to tap on our growing pool of senior workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about plans to harness the potential of our senior workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government will provide support to employers who want to improve their HR capabilities to manage an ageing workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers can tap on the Part-Time Re-employment Grant (PTRG), which we extended last year to support more flexible work options for senior workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As of December 2023, with the support of PTRG, more than 6,300 employers committed to provide part-time re-employment under their HR policy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is expected to benefit around 50,000 senior workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The PTRG also supports employers in implementing structured career planning (SCP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SCP is a process where employers systematically engage their employees and plan out their training and career development goals to align with business needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is particularly useful for employees who are approaching retirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Through PTRG, employers can access free training to learn how to conduct SCP with their employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers can also receive support through the Senior Employment Credit (SEC).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The SEC provides wage offsets to employers who hire Singaporean workers aged 60 and above.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, supporting seniors to remain in the workforce is not just a matter of creating job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Most senior workers today are re-employed in the same job role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But with longer lifespans and careers and a faster pace of economic change, we should not expect to perform the same job role year after year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Senior workers must also keep pace with changes in the labour market and be open to learning new skills or trying out new roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is very good news that we are adjusting the EP qualifying salary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It will help our younger Singaporeans to get jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Does making access to EPs easier via the SOL undermine our efforts to localise or bring in more of our Singaporeans into these jobs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Dr Koh, it is very good news to adjust the $600 matching to $2,000, I think it will help a lot of the lower-wage Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: My point is on the $20,000 lifetime care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And under what circumstances will MOM look to lifting or adjusting this cap?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, as I have shared earlier on, the COMPASS framework was only implemented on 1 September 2023.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, our statistics have been based out of five months.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, in my earlier reply to the Leader of the Opposition, I had qualified that this is very preliminary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we are seeing very early, promising signs that it is a mechanism that did not, in any way, hinder firms, particularly firms wanting to grow their talent and particularly in sectors where there is a shortage of workers today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The measures that we put in place include working with the industry and tripartite partners to constantly curating that list.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, we can add on or remove on a yearly basis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To that end, there are also newer areas where the sectors are fairly nascent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I mentioned two: one is in the green economy, and the other is agri-tech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In those areas, while we allow bonus points for these companies or businesses to bring in foreign talents, we are also simultaneously ramping up our investments to train, upskill and ensure that the skillsets are being transferred to our locals as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is a multi-system moving along to ensure that whatever we lean forward on, that shortage would be alleviated because our locals would then step in to replace that virtuous ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I understand that it may not help all eligible seniors meet their BRS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The fact is that it is not meant to do that.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is actually part of a whole suite of measures, including other schemes, that support retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, the Majulah Package, as well as the SSS , will also help to boost the retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think we are just encouraging everyone to look at this as a means which can catalyse more support for our seniors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not meant to bridge the gap with the BRS.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Tan, you wish to add some more points?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Apologies, I just wanted to remind Members of the House and, in particular, Mr Desmond Choo, that notwithstanding the SOL, all companies, when they bring in an EP, have to fulfil the minimum qualifying salary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That qualifying salary, as I have just shared, would be raised for an entry-level EP and the EP qualifying salary would also rise accordingly with age.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that is the base and after they have fulfilled the base, the SOL, the bonus points would kick in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, in that sense, we continue to ensure that companies do not use it to circumvent whatever framework and principles that we have.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are at least nine Members who have raised your hands.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Anyone who attempts to make a speech, I will cut you off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick question, for the companies that currently pay retrenchment benefit, how many of them pay more than the recommended retrenchment benefits as listed by the tripartite partners?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I confirm with the Minister that the Ministry is going to continue publishing surveys on retrenchment benefit every four years?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not have all the numbers with me currently.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will revert with regards to his question on whether they pay over the recommended retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the ongoing surveys, we hope to sharpen the survey each time we conduct it, using the insights that we have from previous surveys to make it even more precise, because it allows us to better plan our policies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I said, we will constantly work hard at improving the livelihoods for all of our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I have two questions for Senior Minister of State Zaqy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Second, what are the other measures that MOM has put in place to improve workplace safety outcomes and shape the behaviour of both employers and workers?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Indeed, last year we had a challenging period when we had to implement the heightened safety period (HSP) because of the high spate of fatalities during that period.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As I shared, in 2023, we improved the situation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think that this, in itself, hopefully, gives us the first step in terms of our measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What is key is to sustain this, to keep below one per 100,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because after you get there, you do not want to be called a one-hit wonder.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You hope to be like Taylor Swift, with 20 years of success.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Another Member spoke about how we need to put in WSH representatives, but I think that itself may not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have been on enforcements with some of our MOM officers as well on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: When you speak to some of the leaders who have contravened our regulations, some of the comments that come back from business owners or even directors are that of, "Hey, I had my safety audit done, this was done by someone," and it cannot be that way.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you want to create a safety culture, it has to come from the top.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think there are shifts in enforcement and regulations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On top of that, I think we are moving towards more use of technology.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And very soon, we are also putting in analytics to layer on top of this with the use of AI, because we want to make it more effective and more productive, so that our workforce and our workplaces can be safer.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But certainly, I would welcome if NTUC would like to enforce and encourage, or strongly mandate, its employers to also put in WSH representatives, especially from the Labour Movement, to push forward the agenda to make sure that all our workplaces, especially unionised companies, take the lead and set shining examples for industries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I appreciate that there are practical considerations that lead to the need for flexibility on whether non-compete clauses should be allowed for mid-level employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But surely, he would agree with me that the default should be that these clauses do not apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, the Government routinely imposes hard thresholds for all manners of policies and relaxes them through an appeals system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It strikes me as much more efficient and consistent with worker rights if these were discouraged by default, with special cases allowed into tailored employment contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For Minister of State Gan, would the Ministry be able to explain why childcare leave is a legal entitlement, but eldercare leave is not?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Again, I am not speaking up against childcare leave, but is the Ministry implicitly sending some signal that childcare is privileged relative to elderly care?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Work from home arrangements, while an important complement to family care leave, should not be a substitute for those days where flexible work, as useful as it is, does not quite offer the same freedom as actual paid leave.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there is no way to have a default restriction against a restriction of trade clauses for a particular job.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Unless there is a standard job that is available for which we know what a worker does from one company to the next, it is very hard to prescribe in law what the default position is.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Which is why the Court takes a case-by-case approach but lays out principles in which why some of these clauses are non-enforceable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And that is why it is so difficult to have a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The job title of a clerk in one company can mean one thing in one company and mean another thing in another company.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is very hard for us a priori to determine what is the default baseline for a job requirement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: First of all, the Government recognises that caregiving of parents is an important responsibility, especially with Singapore's ageing population.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are committed to providing caregivers with the necessary support so that they can fulfil both their work and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think we need to get this straight.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And I am sure the House agrees with this position.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Even without any legislated mandatory requirement, many progressive employers have already stepped up to introduce caregiving-related leave provisions beyond what is currently mandated, as part of the HR strategy to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think this is likely because FWAs are sustainable and provide flexibility in meeting diverse caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For instance, if a family member requires assistance with daily activities, such as medication and meals, FWAs will be more useful than leave in enabling caregivers to meet those needs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government has also strengthened other areas of support for caregivers of seniors, including those who have to juggle between work and caregiving roles.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Caregivers can tap on a range of care services, such as home and day care, to support the care and social needs of their elderly loved ones.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are also various respite care options in senior care centres and nursing homes to help caregivers look after their seniors for short periods of time, including over the weekends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: My clarifications are around the topic of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: One, with the closure of the SA, could MOM clarify what happens to CPF members who have made CPF investments using their SA?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Two, the Majulah Package should not be limited to those born in 1973 or earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can I ask the Ministry whether they would consider extending this to the younger cohorts when they reach 50 years old in the future?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members may, of course, continue to invest their OA savings under the CPFIS (OA) if they are eligible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Can I request the Member to repeat his second clarification?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I do not think that it should be limited to those born in 1973 or earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: So, will the Ministry consider extending this to younger cohorts when they reach 50 in the future?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Yip's point, successive generations of Singapore Citizens have seen improvements in their lives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is in tandem with Singapore's economic growth and also significant investments made by our Government in education, healthcare and social security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those born in the generation between 1960 and 1973 and earlier had lower incomes over their lifetimes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They also have less time to benefit from the more recent improvements to the CPF system, and they have less runway to build up their retirement savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, younger cohorts would have a longer runway to benefit from the more recent enhancements to the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, the extra interest on CPF accounts, the WIS scheme and all the CCPs that we put up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We constantly and will continually review the need to provide additional support for Singapore Citizens with greater needs, especially when they draw near to retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we look at it today, even for those generations, for instance, the Pioneer or Merdeka Generations, and for the low-wage workers, we continue to enhance the WIS scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations, we continue to enhance the SSS and the MRSS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier on, I gave a list for each one of the schemes, how many hundreds of thousands of Singaporeans will benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, existing eligible Singapore Citizens will benefit, even if they do not meet the age criterion for the Majulah Package.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Chairman, my question is actually to Senior Minister of State Koh.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: I understand that some of the measures that will be introduced will strengthen vulnerable workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: So, I would like to ask if one of the measures would include actually reviewing the 2018 Tripartite Workgroup Recommendations for Self-Employed Persons, because I feel that there is a need to be more affirmative in how we address these vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: My clarification is for Minister of State Gan.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Can the Tripartite Guidelines for Flexible Work Arrangement Requests take into account jobs for which FWAs are deemed not appropriate due to business reasons and require employers to explore and provide alternatives to workers in these job roles, such as more time off or more caregiving leave?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: And also, how does MOM intend to enforce the Tripartite Guidelines given that some errant employers might not choose to comply with these guidelines, given that it is not legislation?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The tripartite partners have recognised that there is no one-size-fits-all approach towards FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I have spoken repeatedly that what works for one company may not work for another.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are different forms of flexible arrangements: flexi-time, flexi-load, flexi-place.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: That said, in designing the Tripartite Guidelines, we are mindful to not take an overly rigid approach that risks creating an adversarial workplace culture.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Preserving this mutual trust and understanding between employers and employees is important for the FWAs to be sustainable.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employers will need to see that FWAs make business sense, that it helps them to attract and retain workers or lead to a productive workforce for them to sustain the practice of providing FWAs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As such, we will continue to educate and equip employers on the implementation of various types of FWAs so that they can identify and provide the appropriate flexibilities that are feasible, taking into consideration business operations while also supporting the employees' needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The first is that it is hard not for some to see it as a form of carry trade whereby the Government is borrowing at 2.5%, 4% from Singaporeans while the GIC makes 7%, both of which in the long-term.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, the question is: if we already have the CPFIS, can we not allow Singaporeans to co-invest part of their savings?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Second, on LRIS, I recognise the Minister's point about risk and that was what the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But in the advisory panel report, they have also noted that this can be overcome via the use of the glide path of the Lifecycle Fund.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, would the Minister not agree that with the implementation of LRIS, at least based on the numbers they suggested, this would be beneficial for Singaporeans in the long-term?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I assume the Member has directed that question at myself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the first part, in terms of the difference between GIC returns and CPF interest rates that both Mr Louis Chua and Ms Hazel Poa talked about, this has been discussed earlier at the debate on the Motion on Public Finances on 7 February 2024.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not want to go too much into details.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But it is always very easy from the point of investment to look at hindsight because hindsight is perfect.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have done a lot of investments in my past life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are a lot of "I should have done this" and "I should have done that".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We need to understand that while GIC's historical 20-year returns have exceeded CPF interest rates, this is really looking at it backwards.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Above all, I think Mr Louis Chua, as a financial analyst, it is always very good to look at past historical records.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But to make a projection in the future, I seriously wonder how many people can be that spot-on and precise in terms of projecting future returns and on a guaranteed basis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I have said before that since CPF started in 1955, the three core priorities are: (a) to fund retirement adequacy for our members; (b) to provide housing; and (c) healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's LRIS point, we said we are not putting it in abeyance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have considered and we continue to consider in terms of making sure that the returns are stable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the last three to four years, the Member, as an analyst, would also agree with me, does he not, that we have gone through an extremely uncertain and volatile period?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I take the Member's nodding of the head as a yes, right?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For us, it is making sure that the hard-earned monies of every single one of our CPF members, we try to go to the n-th degree to try to make sure that it is stable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We try to make sure that we reduce as much of the volatility and the risk as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Maybe, if the Member wants to put it as a fault – I do not think it is a fault – it is that we are very, very cautious because these are our members' hard-earned monies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that the Member acknowledges and understands that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have five minutes to our guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will try to squeeze in two more clarifications.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Can I ask the Minister if he can share the main findings and also, is MOM incorporating the findings into the policies?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister, I hope your reply will not be too long.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are seven of you who raised your hands but, unfortunately, I am going to give the last clarification to Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Besides electricians, there are many other skilled trades and many of them are having an ageing workforce as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I ask what is the Ministry's timeline to uplift all the trades?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And a broader point of clarification is: is the Ministry tackling the problem of an ageing workforce, low wages, heavy reliance on foreign workers and lower interest in skilled trades among our young with sufficient urgency, or is the Ministry confident that we will continue to have a constant stream of young foreign workers to meet the manpower needs of industry?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, the Member's two clarifications will take some time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are quite confident that we can implement it with a very clear set of deliverables, and there is scalability, meaning that we can extend it to more job roles, given our aspirations for sustainability and the green economy pivot to a greener future for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is a short answer to the Member's question.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will apply the same principles to some of the other trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In time to come, I will update Members of this House.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the point about how we scale up our local workforce to continue to make sure that they are well-prepared and well-skilled, we will continue to invest in them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If I may, I will tell the Member a story because I want to articulate this in a clearer fashion and connect the dots together for the Member.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, from time to time, and at different stages, we rely on the foreign workforce that comes in here to supplement and to complement our Singapore Core.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: How do we walk every step with our fellow Singapore Citizens?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you are a youth and if you have started your career, we empower you to make informed career decisions so that you have a good start.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through working closely with our IHLs, we have developed meaningful internships.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have educational and career guidance as they start out in the workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Then, when you are a mid-career worker looking at next steps, we will help you to pick up and we will invest in you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We provide greater support for you to pick up relevant skills.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also have the SEC and the PTRG, and we are also making sure that our Majulah Package continues to support them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, you can see that it is really an end-to-end, very comprehensive, integrated continuum of uplifting, supporting, strengthening and caring for our entire Singapore Core.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With that, I thank Members of the House for your patience and your support.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Choo, can I invite you to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, I would like to thank Minister Tan See Leng, Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon and Minister of State Gan Siow Huang for the very thoughtful and comprehensive responses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Of course, to Permanent Secretary Ng Chee Khern and his team of MOM officers for their tireless work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
